en: Table of Contents for the Recorded Sayings of Master Qiaoyin,
Volume One:
Recorded Sayings from his Second Tenure at Chongsheng Chan Temple on Xuefeng Mountain.
Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Qiāoyǐn, Volume One: Including Dharma Talks, Postscripts, Verses,
Liturgical Rites, and Other Matters from the Lower Volume.
Record of the Words of the Master upon Re-entering Xuefeng Chongsheng Chan Monastery, compiled by Attendant Zhengding.
On the first day of the intercalary third month in the first year of the Yanyou era, the Master entered the monastery. He received [the ceremonial items].
The Imperial Decree states: "At the Phoenix Gate, spring is lush; atop Mount Ao, the snow has cleared. Without seeking anything for oneself, it arrives from Heaven.
It flows forth from the breast, covering heaven and earth."
The *Jianghu Shu* (Draft on Rivers and Lakes). It takes the myriad phenomena of the universe as a single tongue. But tell me: is this slander or praise?
The *Du Shu* says: "It is all contained within."
Pointing to the Dharma-seat, [Xuefeng said]: "The entire earth is gathered together to form a single precious Lotus-King Seat;
all people in the world have their share of gazing upon it. Today, Xuefeng ascends higher step by step. Should you hesitate for even a moment, the seat itself will seize you."
[The Master] lifts the incense for the Emperor’s longevity. This single offering of incense cannot be buried within the snowy caverns; its fragrance permeates the Nine Palaces.
Upon the withered old logs, new sprouts and shoots take root once more, and its aroma rises to the Imperial Capital.

This servant-monk Wuyi, having this morning reverently received the Imperial Grace to continue serving as the Abbot of Xuefeng Chongsheng Chan Temple in Fuzhou Prefecture, [offers this] on the occasion of opening the hall. From afar...
Beholding the Golden Palace, I burn this precious incense burner above, solely to pray for the long life of the present Emperor—
ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! May Your Majesty, the Emperor,
graciously grant that you live for eight thousand autumns and eight thousand springs, as the *chūn* tree flourishes beneath the heavens of Yao.

The shadow [of the tree] lasts for three thousand years; its flowers bloom for three thousand years, and its fruit ripens for three thousand years. The *pántáo* (peaches of immortality) wafts their fragrance through the Imperial Gardens.
May this fragrance be offered on behalf of the various Prime Ministers and State Dukes of the Zhongshu Sheng and Xuanzheng Yuan, to augment their longevity and official emoluments.
I humbly pray that the Supreme Chancellor, the Pivot of the Origin, shall rectify the hundred officials and harmonize the Yin and Yang through imperial governance;
may the Buddha-Dharma flourish once more, remaining as a steadfast pillar for ten thousand years.
This single incense offering is respectfully presented to the Yuan-shuai Fu, the Lian-fang Si, the Wan-hu Fu, and the Tong-zhuan of the Fujian Dao.

The Prefecture, together with its subordinate officials, respectfully requests that their stipends and provisions be increased. We pray that as they divide their duties and distribute their offices, the multitude of worthy men may be arrayed like stars;

that all the eminent talents of Zhou and Shao shall proclaim the transformative teachings and carry forth the current of civilization, so that the eight commanderies may bask in the spring-like harmony of the supreme governance of Cheng and Kang.
This single portion of incense was originally intended for deep concealment within crags and caverns, not vying with the profusion and splendor of peach and plum blossoms.

Yet, unexpectedly, by the winds of heaven from the leaking pond, it remains difficult to grasp or contain. Having now brought it forth for this occasion, I burn it within the incense burner as an offering.
Formerly he resided at Mount [Name], and later he resided at Jingci as the late Master Fuxin Dahe-shang.
He established this [teaching] to repay the boundless kindness of the Dharma-milk (the answer and question are not recorded).
As for the guiding principle: if one conforms, one does not abide; if one abides, one does not conform. The void is clear in Beihan; the vermilion phoenix soars aloft. The mountain does not...

When one becomes a person, one emerges as a person. When wind and rain come, the Sleeping Dragon of Nanyang stirs with vigor. When the worthy and virtuous appear, the multitude descends like a flock of birds;
when the call is heard, they arrive in silence. From the rainbow-hued heights they come; even in the deep abyss, none remain dormant. (He picks up the staff. Look, look!

The Great Treasure of the Sovereign descends from heaven; the clouds part to reveal the moon atop the Turtle-peak. The Great Treasure of the Dharma-Master is made manifest in the darkness; the flowers bloom.
The springtime waters of the mountain stream; the *Guangling San* with its broken strings, now resumed in the *Langtao Sha*.

With old melodies newly transposed, the True Teaching is thus proclaimed and spread, and the Heart-Essence of the Buddha is thus transmitted. Heaven opens and earth is laid bare; wind follows and clouds follow.
The chariots and books are unified, and the literary standards and tracks are made one.
Master Faideng said: "Originally, I intended to dwell by cliffs and beside valleys, living in seclusion until my time had passed.
However, because my predecessor Qingliang has a case that remains unresolved, I have come forth today to settle it for him."
The Master held up [the case] and said: "Old man Fadingeng knew only how to maintain what was full and preserve what was achieved, yet he lacked the great ambition to carry on the ancestral legacy.

This mountain monk also wished to hide away by the crags and valleys to pass his time, but because my late teacher, Old Man Foxin, previously resided on this mountain, there remains an unfinished case. Today, I cannot help but come forth once more."
I have deliberated on this for you: to see what is right and not act upon it is a lack of courage.
[The Master] thanked the new and old officials of both ranks and ascended the hall. He cited the Venerable Linji’s address to the assembly, which said:
"I wish to establish the fundamental tenets of Huangbo; you all must assist me in bringing them to completion. At that time, there were two monks present, Kefu and Puhua.
He came out to prostrate, and the Master struck him. The Master said, "Under Linji’s single word, those who mastered his pivot were but one or two.
How few indeed are the men of Lu! Here at Xuefeng, all from Pūrvavideha in the east and Aparagoyānī in the west—fishes and dragons, horns and heads—have gathered together at once.
Each abides in its own position, each attends to its own task; thus they advance and retreat."
By means of ritual, water and milk share a single source—this is indeed so. While there is certainly the establishing and the dismantling, what is the ultimate purport?
*Tut!* The world arises as flowers bloom.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is the first phrase? Feng remained silent for a long while. Later, the monk related this to Changsheng.
Changsheng said, "This is the second phrase. He then asked, "What is the first phrase? Changsheng said: [and remained silent].
“Blue sky! Blue sky! The Master said, “Xuefeng stands atop the highest peak; Changsheng walks upon the deepest ocean floor.
Although these two great elders were thus, they nevertheless did not yet know the first phrase. If someone asks this mountain monk what the first phrase is, [I would say]:
“When the weather is fine, everyone is invited to help drag the timber.”
On the first day of the fourth month, returning from the city, he ascended the hall and said: "The Way is not outside of things; its intent lies right before one's eyes.
At the crossroads of the street, one rides an ox into the bustling market; atop the solitary peak, one looks up and counts the rafters of the roof.
Patting its back, one seeks a copper coin—let people laugh at you as mad and deranged as you please."

Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath on the eighth day of the fourth month: In the Tuṣita palace and the den of ignorance, through kalpas of abiding and kalpas of emptiness, heads emerge and submerge.
On this very day every year, there is a basin of hot water; yet in the end, it washes away the dust but cannot cleanse the bones. *A!* Buddha! Buddha!

Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat. Holding up the staff, [the Master] said: "The Way exists in the weeds and wild grass; though the Dharma is the Dharma, its manifestation is everywhere. The eyes of Rong are all true. The Way exists in the tiles and rubble;
from the soles of the feet to the tops of the feet, light is emitted that shakes the earth. Take one step forward, and you kick through the crown of the skull of Old Śākyamuni.
Take one step back, and you tread upon the ghostly eyes of all the patriarchs of antiquity. Such is the practice of *jinzu* (summer retreat). I look toward...
The moon beside the pavilion of the prefecture; thus one dwells in summer retreat. Clouds atop Mount Wushi: they shine forth with spiritual clarity of their own accord.
Light and object both forgotten, serene and without mind, they roll out and gather in without hindrance. To go on just like this—the mountain monk’s staff, for its part, has not yet let you pass.
(He strikes the ground with the staff. Linji’s Three Mysteries and Fushan’s Nine Bonds.
Ascending the hall for the commencement of the summer retreat: Those who come from Tianping and spend the summer here have no leisure for me to deliberate with you;
those who come from Langye and spend the summer here have no leisure for me to transform you.
Whether it be earth or sand, whether true or false—your mental arrangements remain beneath the bright window.
On the first day of the fifth month, he ascended the hall to express his gratitude to the donors and the newly arrived brothers. "The entire earth is this gate of liberation;
they follow one after another and shoulder to shoulder. The iron pivot has no eyes. The entire earth is all my patrons; the clouds and rivers flow on."
Gold flows along its flanks; wild grasses and mountain flowers shift with the changing seasons. Pine winds and stream waters resound with vibrant form and color.

In this era of great prosperity and auspicious timing, five hundred years have coincided with a rare gathering. Where the dragon’s arrival came to rest, the ancient prophecy of three thousand mouths remains ever fresh.
The local deity of Songshan has renewed the wind and moon; at the Nantipin Stupa, the mists and clouds are once again transformed. This is the Secret Chamber.
The mud is deep; the dark portals are set with pits. The long streets are filled with water, and fire flows through the void.
(Zhuozhuzhang) At just such a time as this, Great Master Zhenjue arose from meditative concentration with composure.

Together with Fuling, Zhanbei, Geyu, Jingqing, and their peers, he now, at the tip of this mountain monk’s staff, speaks for you all of the four phases: formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
[He holds up his staff. "If you understand it this way, all marks are not dharmas. [He lays the staff across his shoulder.

"If you do not understand it this way, all dharmas are not marks. When it is neither of these, how is it? [He strikes the ground with the staff. "At the side of the Wangzhou Pavilion, we once again took hands;
all were people who had attended the old assembly at Kaiping."

At the conclusion of the session, he spoke these verses: The snow-capped鳌 (Aoluo) leans against the void as the azure sky opens; Within it dwells an ancient Buddha named Zhengjue (True Enlightenment).

He scoops up a single ladleful and dragons and elephants rush forth; He rolls three balls that resound through seas and mountains. Whether following conditions or not following them, there is nothing to be attained;
Abiding in marks or being markless is but a mere name and appearance. I vow to take a drop of this cold spring water To wash away the turbidity of the dust-ages in the darkened path.
The wooden man dances and the wooden horse neighs; year after year they come again, their affection not diminished.
With the resolve to practice everywhere like Sudhana, one need have no fear that the green mountains lack pavilions.
Incense is offered on the anniversary of the Great Master Zhenjue. Under Deshan’s staff, nothing can be added or subtracted; beneath Yantou’s phrase, the measure remains unshakable.
Though the kalpa-fire blazes fiercely, this does not perish. Covering heaven and earth, it becomes ever more extraordinary as it emerges.
The incense seems to hover over the Egg-Stupa; auspicious mists gather around Nanti. The full shade and coolness reside entirely within the branches of the *càtóng* tree.
Master Chengshan of Baozangyan in Taizhou arrived. He ascended the hall. (At this time, he was at Dongchan Temple completing the printing of the Tripitaka.
The public case of Pipa Rock is fully resolved; the songs of the Three Vehicles have ceased. At Baozangyan, new achievements surpass all previous eras.
With nine fathoms of earth, the mountain is complete. The white horse neighs in the cold; the journey ahead is not far. The golden cock crows at dawn; the traveler’s dream is shattered. The snow—
When Feng spoke thus, what was his intention? (He struck the meditation staff.
A monk was sent by the lecturer Kaiyuan Yejing to deliver a cup of wine to the temple; he went everywhere until he reached the hall. "A guest comes from afar, leaving me this inch-long jade tablet.
Within it are four characters, each character without consciousness. If you can recognize them, I grant that you are a man."
Dragging Mount Zizhi, he vies with Elephant Bone Peak for the forehead. If you have not yet recognized this, (he raises the staff) let me, the staff-bearer, once more rub and polish it for you.
(He strikes the ground with the staff) Dragon slumbers at the phoenix palace; tigers leap upon the celestial thoroughfare. At the end of the summer retreat, a brief instruction:
For two thousand years of Buddha-dharma, spring is cold and autumn is hot; within these ninety days in the mountains, the night is dark.
The day is bright. The study of meaning and the study of the profound are dimly visible; Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment are vivid and numinous.
A wooden boat floats as the waves of Mount Sumeru surge; an iron ship floats as the waves of the great earth tilt. Cultivating non-cultivation, that which was to be done is finished;
realizing non-realization, what was to be accomplished is complete. A single mechanism does not move, and ten thousand transformations subside. (Zhuo)
The Master said: "Whose mortar and pestle is sending forth the sound of autumn?
He raised the case of Ba Ling Huashang, who asked a monk: "Have you come to tour the mountains, or have you come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma? The monk said:

"In this world of peace and tranquility, what need is there to speak of the Buddha-dharma? Ba Ling said: "What a fine 'unconcerned' Chan guest you are! The monk said: "That is already quite a lot of concern."
"I understand. Lingyun said, "Upādyāya, you spent the summer retreat here last year. The monk said, "I did not.
Lingyun said, "Since we did not know each other before, get down from here. The commentary states: Lingyun was a first-generation descendant of Xuefeng.

In his responses to the master’s interrogation and discernment, he still possessed the majestic spirit of his ancestor. However, it was simply improper for him to treat the Buddha-dharma as mere social courtesy.
When a monk enters a door, although his speech and appearance may be impressive, his ritual etiquette is ultimately flawed.
Consider, for instance, the final words of Master Bashi Ling: "I did not know you before; go down. What was his intention?
"Three cups of wine to entertain the guest; one song to sing at the head."

On the first day of the eighth month, he ascended the hall to express his gratitude to the Chief Administrator (Tiandiandian) of Mount Jing and the Guest Master (Zhike) of Jiangxin Temple. "A year’s worth of lifting and half a year’s worth of lifting:

when you point, you do not arrive; when you arrive, you do not point. When guest and host are both complete, the night moon over Zhongchuan is bright and the autumn clouds at the Twin Peaks (Shuangjing) have withdrawn.
"Xuefeng speaks thus—do you know where it lands? *Psh!* I shall meet you before the Sangha Hall."
On the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall. He cited the episode of Nanquan and Zhaozhou while admiring the moon. Nanquan said, "When will it ever be like this?
Zhaozhou then brushed his sleeves and walked away. The Master offered this verse: Two palace maidens, tipsy on pipes and strings, Their lingering emotions dwell mostly beyond the Nine Heavens.
Within the fragrant shadows of the cassia tree, they shift their steps lightly, Competing with Lady Chang'e for youthful grace.
On the first day of the ninth month, [the Master] ascended the hall to take his leave of the former Head Seat of the Eastern Hall, who was concurrently the Head Seat of Xichan Lantian.
"My Head Seat has been traveling," he said. "A crimson phoenix soars through the high heavens. My Head Seat has arrived; with a single cast, he has hooked six giant turtles.
His spiritual mechanism manifests through its function, and his realization rises as his person does. As the spring gushes forth, the mountain stream at night adds to the waves."

Commissioned by the Xuanzheng Yuan, he ascended the hall upon returning from his visit to Gushan Temple. He proclaimed the circulation of virtuous governance throughout the north of Yan and the south of Min.
At Shimen Pass, the low-lying heights cradle the night moon; along Tongxiao Road, the dark paths lock in the clear mists. With the striking of staffs and the shouting of "Ho!"—
How can either of them bear it? Xuefeng wins out by letting loose his foolishness.
At the Small Assembly for the Winter Solstice: "The Buddhas do not appear in the world; the Way of the superior man flourishes. Bodhidharma did not come from the West; the way of the petty man wanes.
Continuing the flame and linking the fragrance, one beats the ice to fetch fire. Holding up the single phrase alone and singing it, one cuts through the water to form flowers. —Dongshan.
He cleared away the fruit trays. Being poor, his family could hardly afford vegetarian food. Ciming posted a notice before the hall;
being busy, he did not have time for cursive script. Here at Xuefeng, they bury their heads in construction work—how could they ever know of such matters?
Li Duke at the eastern corridor stacks the capitals upon capitals and the architraves upon architraves; Dr. Chen at the western corridor acts as the pillar.

The foundation serves as the pillar; the beams serve as the rafters. Every mechanism is brought into play; every thing is fully revealed. The cold plum blossoms by the stream naturally waft their fragrance.
[The Master] cites Zen Master Zhijue: Whenever he saw a monk in the corridor, he would clench his fist and show it to him, saying, "The myriad phenomena..."
The myriad phenomena—the grasses, trees, and forests; whether male or female, monk or layperson; mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are entirely contained within this single grasp.
The Master picked it up and said: "The Elder Zhengjue, atop a solitary peak, held his pole in one hand over the Eastern Sea, intending to catch every fish and dragon.
Little did he know that with such vast waves and deep clouds, those who would take the hook were few."
"Xuefeng tonight will test those who can take one look. (With the gesture of casting a fishing line with his staff) "Examine it closely, examine it closely!

[He ascends the hall. (Narration) He thanks the two ranks of officials. Ye Er has arrived for a brief visit. (He is able to paint dragons and tigers. He raises the Dharma banner and establishes the fundamental tenets.
Those on the same path seek one another; those with the same heart assist one another. Why? Because when painting a dragon, one looks at its head; when painting a tiger, one looks at its tail.

When the Buddha ascended the hall upon his attainment of the Way, the fresh snow blanketed the mountains and the morning star shone brightly through the night. In his dire straits, he sought a way to live, yet he could not find a way to distinguish himself.
If, at that time, the Old Man Śākyamuni had been able to utter a different word regarding the cultivation of virtue and the refinement of conduct—* *—[the outcome would have been otherwise].
"Where does the planet Mars stop? From three stations. [He] ascended the hall.
"Yunyan was at Yaoshan for twenty years, single-mindedly clarifying this matter. The donkey chooses a damp spot to urinate.
Zhaozhou sets aside the two times of meal—porridge and rice—and does not allow his mind to be distracted. The dog licks the hot oil pan. At Xuefeng’s place, it has long been..."
Sleeping late and rising leisurely; weary of sitting, strolling at ease—this does not hinder striking the third watch at noon.
[The Master] ascends the hall. Because of the thanks from the guest prefect of Daochang Monastery, [the Master] said: "When Xuefeng first saw a monk, he asked, 'Where have you come from?
The monk replied, 'From Zhejiang. The Master said, 'By boat or by land? The monk said, 'Neither path was traversed. The Master said: [This...]
"Who can reach this place? The monk replied, "Not even a hair’s breadth separates us. The Master then struck him with his staff and drove him out.
The Master commented: "This monk came from the region of Zhejiang; from the moment he entered the gate, his every word was sincere and true.
Why did Xuefeng imitate Deshan’s conduct? 'Once a profligate, one is especially compassionate toward travelers.'"
A Minor Sermon for the Eve of the New Year. Dongshan’s minor sermon did not light a lamp—drawing the horizontal bone out from within the darkness.

Deshan’s minor sermon did not answer a word—sitting with his tongue out in the midst of clarity. He digs into the armpit to expose the breast; he shifts the long to accommodate the short; he carves coins from the tip of a needle.
Competing for inches and struggling over minutes, the eternal reality is already manifest as a lamp and candle. This mountain monk responds according to his capacity:
rolling the Xuefeng ball, heaven turns and earth revolves; beating the Heshan drum, mountains shake and peaks tremble; burning firewood logs, it soars through the present and illuminates the ancient.
They sing the *Village Music*, the *White Snow*, and the *Yangchun*. The wildcat and the white ox laugh with upturned brows.

One year is subtracted, one year is added. (He raises the whisk. Is there anyone who does not undergo this reckoning of years? (He strikes the whisk. The plum blossoms add to the spring; the snow is white.
The willow branches are green amidst the morning mist.
Master Ying’an cited a monk who asked Xianglin, “What is the matter beneath the patched robe?
Xianglin replied, “In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains. Xianglin speaking thus is much like a rat entering a corner; it is as if someone were asking Guizong.
"What is this matter beneath the patched robe? [The Master] simply said to him: "Next year there will be new branches;
the spring wind’s vexation shall never cease. The Master commented: "When these two great elders spoke thus, one who had grasped it said he had not, and one who had not grasped it said he had.
Examining them closely, both were lacking one point. Someone asked: [Why was this?]
Xuefeng was asked, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? He simply replied to him: "This year ends tonight;
next year begins tomorrow.

On the occasion of the New Year, he ascended the hall and said: "Spring moves through the capital; grace descends from the nine heavens. On this day when the True Origin opens and prospers, joyful matters have already occurred."
First, the Transmission. Why? On the *renzi* day of the first ten days [of the lunar month]—(the *Renzi* New Year)—there will be a bountiful year.
On the Lantern Festival, he ascended the hall: "Brilliantly clear, yet pitch-black; the true lamp illuminates the world. Rong’s eyes shine with a chilling light.
Do not look upon Mount Ao through mist and rain."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: (This is an expression of gratitude to the Elder Yunmen Bin, as well as a response to the letter of succession from Guangtong in Chaozhou.
"The letter is received; the message is received. A crocodile from the South Sea has horns upon its head; a turtle-nosed snake from the Southern Mountain swallows the void with its mouth.
This is still merely a phrase concerning the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching. But as for what was said within that letter—what matter is it? "Coming to the mountain, one sees the boat."
Disciple. Yunmen succeeded Xuefeng. He ascended the hall and said:

"Moment after moment there is no stopping; from instant to instant there is no abiding. Delusion and enlightenment are two paths; one must suddenly reach the ultimate through the total functioning [of the mind].
After Lingyun departed, who will discuss this? On the branches of the peach blossoms, red rain falls."

Ascending the hall for the opening ceremony: The dragon towers are warm with clouds; the phoenix palace is thick with spring. The great trichiliocosm is unified; carriages and books are blended as one.
But ultimately, how does Xuefeng offer his benediction? (He strikes the sounding staff. The Sun rises from the east of Fusang;

the Buddha enters Nirvana. Ascending the hall: The den of karma in the city of Kuśinagara is leveled; the waters of craving in the Hiraṇyavatī River are drained. The fragrance of freedom from sorrow...

The tree is old; in the garden of awakening, fallen petals lie deep. A handful of idle sorrows grows cold within my heart. The singing of the wandering oriole reaches the very sound that breaks the heart.

Incense is offered on the anniversary of the passing of the former Master, the Buddha-mind. One person’s spring is shallow; the ancient ravine’s spring is deep. Dropping into the water, there is no entanglement.
Deep is the grace, deep is the sorrow. Why today do you present *ping* and *zao* offerings? Why burn *shuishen* incense?
*A!* A broken mirror harbors a heart of the five rebellious acts.
On the first day of the month, he ascends the hall to frame the Buddha-dharma; within the snap of a finger, he manifests the Hall of Universal Radiance. Great achievement is not...

The Abbot manifested a sixteen-foot golden body upon a single blade of grass; the Dharma-commands were fully revealed, the clouds parted from the elephant’s tusk, and the cold spring surged in the springtime.
(He strikes the meditation staff. "Covering heaven and covering earth, behold this new style!
Entering the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: the water strikes the golden basin; the skin is as smooth as a jade lotus. Pure wisdom is perfectly luminous, and the numinous light shines alone."
The Golden Wheel bathes in the dawn light of Fusang.

[He] ascends the hall to express his gratitude for the Head Seat’s holding of the whisk. This very function is detached from this function; master and guest are fully present, capturing and releasing at will.
A whisk made of tortoise hair weighs as much as ten thousand catties.
Baoyun Pínglù Wàoshàng arrived. He ascended the hall and, citing the case of Baoyun Zhì Wàoshàng meeting Xuánshā, said:
Xuánshā asked him, "Why have you come? Zhì replied, "I have come specifically to see the Master. Xuánshā asked, "After we have met, what then?
Zhì said, "I shall wait to display my family style. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "When Yun entered the gate of Xuánshā, in the mere instant of their first meeting, he immediately spoke."

One must be able to fully display the family style. It is like presenting jade in ritual and setting forth bells and drums in music; that the prosperity of the Three Dynasties was recorded upon silk is precisely this.
Today, when Xuefeng and Master Baiyun meet, alas, their sleeves are too short for their arms.
Though they wish to fully display the family style, in the end they find themselves at a loss for how to act. Nevertheless, "when one's house is poor, one hopes for a wealthy neighbor."

Ascending the hall on the second day of the fifth month for the anniversary of the Patriarch’s passing: first ascending the Snowy Ridge is like entering the Passes with the maps and records already secured;
where the Dragon comes to rest is like the gate of Mengchang, where three thousand guests were fed.

Rolling the three balls, amidst the miasmic smoke and pestilential rains, he raises the tip of the ladle—like black aconite and arsenic—to unleash the function of Deshan’s staff. The golden [sword] of Ya Fu...
The drum resounds, continuing the flame of the paper lanterns of Longtan; Tian Dan’s fire-oxen and Fayen’s branching schools, the arrow of Silla passing through, and the Yunmen lineage arrayed.

The command is enforced throughout Wu and Yue; the pagoda-seal is spring-like in its melting radiance. Incense thickens within the chamber of repose, and auspicious mists gather over the pines of the mountain.
The floral structure is newly formed; the clay ox roars at the moon as ten thousand mountains grow cold. The wooden horse neighs in the wind as a thousand ridges break into dawn.
Speaking in this manner, let it be left to you all to paint the picture beneath these words.
Yet, as for what the Patriarch said: “At Wàngzhōu Pavilion, I have already met you. At Wūshí Ridge, I have already met you. Before the Sangha Hall, I have already met you.”
I have seen it. But what, ultimately, was the intention? (He strikes the table three times. Do not take offense that I have frequently urged you to drink while seated;
since we parted, I have rarely seen you.

Incense is offered on the anniversary of the Patriarch’s death. The spring thaws as the pagoda is sealed; the moon is bright upon the pine-covered mountains. The great elegance flows like a riverbank; the flies buzz and the earthworms burrow their holes.
A single melody from Guangling awakens a thousand peaks at dawn.
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth: A spiritual prescription from behind the elbow, a wondrous technique not transmitted; who can distinguish that which kills and that which brings life?
At the bottom of the mountain stream, the calamus grows with nine joints.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] held up his staff and said: "The Great Mirror does not record; the Ultimate Principle transcends words. Why did Linji ask about the Buddha-dharma three times?
Why did Xuefeng go to Dongshan nine times? (He struck the floor once with the staff. "A deer tracks through a rabbit's path."
The tiger devours the remains of the eagle.

Entering the hall in the Central Lands: the secret instructions of all Buddhas and the profound guiding principles of the patriarchs—before the sound and after the phrase, there is nothing with which to deliberate.
The mountains are deep; even in the sixth month, it is cool.

On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, Jian Shenmiao ascended the hall (at a time of great wind and rain). Linji entered the gate and immediately shouted; this is like carrying a jar to water the garden plots.
Deshan entered the gate and immediately struck with his staff; this is like pulling up seedlings to help them grow. This mountain monk does not fall into the ordinary; he alone transcends.
A single phrase from past and present: let me try to bring it forth for you all. Autumn colors ferment; the wind beats against the rain. Springs fill the mountain ravines;
waters surge with the sound of rapids.
Small-scale *chanshi* (private instruction) for the end of the summer retreat. To depart is to be sealed: clouds span Mount Wushan; ten thousand trees cry out in autumn.
To remain is to break the seal: the moon cools the cold spring; a thousand waves divide the reflection. Neither departing nor remaining: a mangy horse guards an empty sock.

it is hard to endure the evening wind and rain. Striking it off at the head of the staff, the snapping turtle gnashes its teeth—at the end of the phrase..."
Accepting this responsibility, the tiger has sprouted wings; its roar resounds through the Southern Kingdoms, shaking the thunder and lightning across ten billion worlds.

The two lineages of the Lamp flame spread their brilliance like the high sun across ten billion heavens and earths. The inscription on the tortoise shell is self-evident, blazing upon the jade tablets and dark ritual axes of gold and stone.
The stupa doors stand wide open, securely placing a cluster of eggs upon great mountains and solid rocks. Though they melt away, they are never exhausted; ice fills [the world].
A long street—there is no door through which to look up and admire. A deep mud pit within a sealed chamber—it covers heaven and earth, not altered by so much as a hair’s breadth.

From antiquity to the present, it has not changed by a hair’s breadth; looking back to the past is like looking at the present, and looking at the present is like looking at the past. At the pine gate, along the single path, flowers lie scattered in profusion.
Offering incense on the anniversary of the Patriarch’s passing: How could De Shan ever have stepped upon the threshold? How could he ever have slept upon the guest-bed at Mount Ao?
Seeing people thus, traveling thus—(lifting up the incense, he says)—how could this mere trifle ever have been smelled?
Tell me, what is it? It resembles the root of a *caitika* tree; it looks like a broken wooden ladle.

Master Xie, the Head Seat, holds the whisk and ascends the hall. (Holding up the staff) Singing and chanting proceed in tandem; principle and phenomena are as one. Mountains are cleared from level ground;
the ocean is drawn from a single drop. But as for Shaoyang’s raising of a single word—how does one penetrate it?
(Brandishing the staff) We all ascend the hall together.
When a pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water becomes clear all at once; when Chan gathers in a distracted mind, the distracted mind becomes settled.
To understand it in this way is precisely to fall into the sickness of students of the present day. What about when it is not like this at all? "If you do not think of it..."
Madness. To cultivate mindfulness is to become a sage.

A small-scale *xichan* (summer retreat) discourse, also expressing thanks to the new and former head seats and the library director. Illumination detached from conditions; the jade palace is clear and pure.
The moon dips into the square pond; phenomena melt into reality. Dew chills the silver bed; the spring connects to the eye of the ocean. Fragrance lingers as the curtain rolls back beyond the eaves;
five feet of space leave no room for heaven. Black stones and clouds hang across the tip of a flying arrow; there is a path to turn the body.

Preaching the Dharma in the celestial palace, one has not yet departed from the teachings; a single character atop the stele adds further to the ancient seal script. If you can see it here, all is but dust.

Throughout the oceans of Buddha-lands, there is nothing that is not the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). It is utterly detached from the signs of sinking into emptiness; it fuses the ten ages of past and present, such that there is nothing that is not the season of self-liberation.
There is no distinction between the new and the old; in a single thought-moment, one completely transcends, and the myriad functions of the mind are stilled and eliminated.
The spiritual void is vast and penetrating; it illuminates all things without leaving a trace. If one is already thus, what then? A rat chasing a monkey.
Shishuang once had two monks arrive at Yangshan. One day, he sighed and said, "There is not a single person here who understands Chan.
One day, while they were working together to carry firewood, Yangshan deliberately dropped some wood and asked, "What did you say? The two [monks]...
The monks remained silent. Yangshan said, "And yet you say that there is not a single person here who understands Chan.
When Yangshan returned, he told this to Guishan, saying, "Those two monks were cross-examined by me. Guishan asked, "How did you cross-examine and penetrate them?"
Yangshan recounted the previous conversation. Baizhang said, "Jizi, you have been exposed by me once again. The Master commented:
"The two monks spoke with the reckless words of the simple-minded; they were like rams butting against a fence. Yangshan was needlessly anxious in a quiet place, like a house dog guarding its den.
Baizhang’s final remark was likewise an attempt to forget his own ugliness."
The Buddha ascends the hall after attaining the Way. Those who cling to things are like mere stars; they cannot escape the karma of hunger and cold.
They do not know the nobility of the imperial yellow palace, yet they take pleasure only in the heights of the Snowy Mountains. Why is this? When color reaches its limit, it returns to black.
The Small Sermon on New Year’s Eve: The true mechanism operates in secret; the heavens speak not, yet the four seasons proceed. The great transformation is applied in obscurity;
the earth speaks not, yet the myriad things are born. Sun, moon, and stars—neither new nor old. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—without change or alteration.
For the patch-robed monks, sitting upon their seats, upon their meditation cushions, they cannot calculate it, they cannot penetrate it, and they cannot evade it.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, the eyes and nostrils remain exactly as they were before. To fill them is difficult; it is a bottomless pit.
[The Master] ascends the hall to thank the new visiting guests and the Abbot of Jiangshan. Movement and stillness are one; host and guest mutually merge.

In the crystal goblet, the incense swirls like snow upon a cold mountain stream; in the ocean of the Flower Treasury, the red blossoms flutter in the wind. Monkeys startle and cranes lament under the moon.
The mountains are clear and empty; the evening snow is heavy, much like the memories of Jiangdong.

On the occasion of the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascends the hall to give a discourse and simultaneously express gratitude to his Dharma relatives: "The peach talismans are nailed high, and the mugwort tigers are hung low; a hundred monsters and a thousand demons [are thus repelled]."
The tracks have been swept away; there is no path. When brothers meet, they do not raise an eyebrow. A single phrase is a vast, undifferentiated whole;
who can complete the old dialogue between guest and host? Sudhana has returned; mountain after mountain is shrouded in cold, as the yellow plum rains fall.

A Small Sermon on the Eve of the Year’s End. The old year wishes to depart but has not yet departed; it is as difficult as trying to control six horses with a frayed rope. The new year wishes to arrive but has not yet arrived;
it is like the Ox-Head Chan Master pushing his cart along with the moon. When one tries to pursue them, they do not move; the red thread remains at one's heels.

When one tries to shake them off, the blue ash stays upon one's head. Yet, one fails to realize that the Way transcends past and present: clouds span Mount Wushan, and the Dharma encompasses all dharmas.
Behold! The waters are solemn against the dark cliffs. For us patch-robed monks, from year’s end to year’s end, it is much like a monkey grasping at shadows.
When the year is spent and the age exhausted, we do not leave our life within the rat’s den. (He strikes the *zhuzhang*. Cold ashes crackle with beans;
spring returns to the great earth. The *zhuzhang* at the head of the bed releases its blossoms.
The Master cited a monk’s question to Master Baiyun: “What is it like when the year is exhausted and the age ends?
Baiyun replied, “The eyebrows are above the eyes. The Master commented: “In responding to the occasion and exchanging words, there is nothing lacking in accordance with principle and reality.
Yet, even Master Baiyun, when scrutinized, still lacks one move. If someone were to ask Xuefeng about the exhaustion of the year and the end of the age...”
How is this so? Simply say to him: "In the mountains there are no drums or horns; the dawn bell is the New Year.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascends the hall: "The golden reed-knee is coldly bursting forth; the frosty night is bright with the splendor of the stars.
For six years he failed to complete his practice; by day he wasted his time on mere wheat and hemp. When Xuefeng speaks thus, is he praising him?
This is disparaging others. Alas! Sand does not stick in the eye. Ascending the hall:
The wind is high, blocking the geese; the dew is cold, and the crickets cry in the courtyard. The old barbarian has needlessly traveled from Wei to Liang;
the autumn pestle idly adds to the length of the night’s pounding.

Ascending the hall: The morning dew brightens the withered leaves; Clear clouds embrace the verdant pines. Those who travel everywhere for instruction do not understand: Autumn deepens across the hundred cities to the south. Ascending the hall:
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? [The Master replied: "Yellow chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge. Study!
Ordinary people do not understand this. On the Double Ninth, the Master offered this verse: At the rustic inn, sparse fences guard the bamboo smoke;
The new fodder is just ripening under the chrysanthemum sky. The host, loath to part, detains his guests; He offers wine at a low price, regardless of the cost.

Entering the five viscera of the Buddha: the Yellow-Faced Old Man, throughout immeasurable kalpas, has repeatedly emerged and submerged from his head, cultivating the karmic causes of ignorance and accomplishing the karmic fruits of ignorance.
This continues even unto the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, devas, humans, Śakras, and Brahmās, all of whom see with the same eyes and hear with the same ears;
each performs their respective karma and each receives a corresponding retribution, until two thousand years have passed.
Later, before the Snowy Peaks and atop the Golden Hall, his heart, liver, and five viscera were each laid bare.
All the people of the world could do nothing but blink their eyes. Today, I, this mountain monk, reach out a single arm for all of you where there is no place to insert a hand.
From the very beginning, I have gathered and set them aside for you; look! (He measures the five viscera. Śākyamuni remains Śākyamuni;
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra remain Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; Kāśyapa and Ānanda remain Kāśyapa and Ānanda;
Śakra and Brahmā remain Śakra and Brahmā. Neither long nor short, neither deficient nor superfluous—throughout antiquity and unto the present, there is no difference.
It is distinct. I hope you will settle your mind in tranquility and stabilize your spirit in stillness—like an empty treasury being empty, like a mirror reflecting a mirror.
Speaking thus, is this to magnify the Buddha’s majestic radiance, or to proclaim the Buddha’s benevolent virtue? It is one color, yet it wins twice over.
Rebuilding the world: the plaque for the Xuefeng Hall. When the great gate of the profound pivot was opened wide, the banner of the Dharma was planted at a time when all lay prostrate upon the earth;
when the ancestral fortune was restored, the great beam of the Law was erected on a day it supported the heavens.

How could this not be so? The Way has neither past nor present; it meets its moment. Awakening has its sequence; a single path leads to the profound. For fifteen hundred years, the dragons have trod upon the clouds.
Tiered eaves pierce the Milky Way; ten billion suns and moons revolve in circles. The mountain streams and pine winds proclaim the Dharma with fervent intensity.

Phoenixes soar and peacocks dance; snowflakes and the Milky Way shine and swirl. By these means, the Sun of the Buddha’s radiance is cleansed and brightened; by these means, it is made eternally majestic.
The imperial foundation. By this, he reveals the true eye of the monks; by this, he opens the gate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Now, as it is held high before us, do you all understand? Throughout the world, Xuefeng is the one whom all look up to.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, the Buddha’s radiance was revealed. In the past, at midnight on the Snowy Mountains, he beheld a star; a single point appeared upon the tip of a hair.
Today, at Xuefeng, he beholds the sun in broad daylight; a pair of eyebrows arches across his brow. Amidst golden light, the golden-haired lion crouches upon the ground.
Within the realm of silver, a jade elephant leaps forth. Ānanda, though possessed of great learning, has not yet distinguished between mud and water; Kāśyapa smiles, his eyes suddenly protruding.
How marvelous, how marvelous! All sentient beings throughout the great earth possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata.
Who is it that gives rise to deluded thoughts, vainly creating birth and extinction? Who is it that clings to them, needlessly painting them in colors?
Now, the wind through the pines plays its melody, and the zither resounds with the sound of mountain streams. Auspicious clouds gather at dawn, and auspicious snow unfolds in the clear sky.

I, this mountain monk, shall now attempt to assist in the manifestation of the meaning of the *dharmatā* (true nature) upon the tip of a single hair. (Holding up his brush, he says: Do you see? Now the Buddha emits a radiance.
Re-entering the ancestral hall to establish the memorial tablets (including those who have already been provisionally included):
here is the ladle already fixed by the successive patriarchs. One cannot add even a single thread; to do so would be to wander in vain. One cannot subtract even a single thread;
to do so would be to labor fruitlessly at drilling and carving. Only one with the extraordinary talent to "pierce the upper story and span the hearth" can truly manifest this trust.

The subtle strategies of the patriarchs have been restored; one might have thought that ashes were cold and fires extinguished, that valleys would change and hills shift, that clouds would disperse and waters flow away, filling the ditches and blocking the gullies.
(Pointing to the plaque) Because there is this slight bit of idle fame, in the end it can never be erased.

A brand-new magnificent structure rises with stars circling its eaves and rafters; the Patriarchal Temple stands like jade, auspiciousness opening across its pavilions and towers. (Passing the plaque) For those without teeth at the bottom...

"Those who have already passed go over there. (He then passes the name-card and says: "One who has no nostrils goes over there. Without distinguishing between Chu and Yue, the jade doors have no pivot;
firmly holding the borders, the iron gates have their keys. (He then passes the name-card again and says: "Allow me, this old monk, to take a step ahead of you."
The donor Zhang crossed the deep ravine and entered the ancestral shrine; (he constructed the Patriarch’s Hall and) Songshan Pavilion, departing from the layered city walls.
A single leaf drifts lightly on the fragrant breeze. Ascending Xueqiao Peak, the blazing clouds have completely dispersed as a thousand peaks awaken at dawn.
The single spiritual true nature harmonizes perfectly whether hidden or manifest; it transcends the three periods of time instantaneously, and its coming and going attain the wondrous.
Moved by a solemn vow, he cast the gold from his pouch to assist in the construction. A brilliant new standard was established, opening a pavilion and a gable within the ethereal clouds.

The mountain-dweller manifested that axe and hatchet leave no trace; with a roar, he swept away the cold ashes of the kalpa’s conflagration. The Wushan Ridge stretches across the void for ten thousand [miles].

The characters were carved into the cliff; though the engraving was not yet finished, Red Pine (Chisongzi) drew his long robes far out and stepped forth amidst this heroic wind without leaving a word of conversation.

The deep ravine branches off from the ancient stream; the moonlight in the mind reflects the brilliance of the pine-moon. The public’s contribution for the Master is clearly manifest before us; the hall enshrining the Master shall perpetuate the lamp-flame forever. When the mountain monk speaks thus, it is all— [Note:

The text appears to be a fragment of a stele inscription or poetic prose concerning a Buddhist site, likely involving a master named "Gong" (the Master). The final phrase "總是" (all are/is) suggests the sentence may continue.]
Painting the shadows of the deep ravine is a matter of secondary concern. As for the phrase, "Without passing through the provisional city, one ascends directly to the precious site"—how is this?
I have been waiting for you at my empty seat for a long time.
The gathering of causes for Huang Yunyan’s burial of his remains:
life is a convergence, death is a dispersal. By day, the long rope cannot bind it; the waters of Penglai are shallow, and the human world is no more.
Illusory and fleeting, everything turns to a dream in the blink of an eye. Not far from home lies Sheshan in spring; dwelling within these mountains is the most excellent of cities.
This dwelling place possesses a family deed with clear evidence: green stone and vermilion script bear the name of the Huang clan.

With the dragon on the left and the tiger on the right, heaven serves as the gate and earth as the door. By this may the house and cottage be blessed; by this may descendants and children receive fortune.

May the brothers be as fragrant as the *dai-e* flower, their branches and leaves flourishing; may the orchids and jade-like children stand in dense array within the courtyard. May the deities guard the mountain forests, ensuring eternal peace and stability.
Ten thousand autumns, ten thousand ages—a single mound of earth.
The Reverend Master Sùwēng enters his stupa. (He resided at seven mountains and was a successor of Yǎnxī.
He revealed the upward-pointing pivot and brought forth the final word. A solitary moon over the three mountains in autumn mist; five li of clouds and mist obscure the view.
On the ancient path, he erected the first Dharma-banner of Abiding Goodness; dwelling in the majestic abode of the Heavenly Kings, he swept the alchemical hearth of the Immortal Ren.
Spiritual radiance shone upon the jade-like grains, and as he boarded the fishing boat of Master Xie, the shadow of his pole brushed against the coral trees.
At the peak of Xuefeng, he causes the mountain stream to flow upstream; at the gate of direct pointing, he restores the ordinary state of affairs.

Whether wandering abroad or returning to seclusion, whether in city or forest, whether regarding birth-and-death or coming-and-going, amidst frost flowers and morning dew—the stupa of Cui Peak has already opened.
"Leaves fall and return to the root"—there are no remaining words. If one goes forth in this very manner, what then? The night in the Land of Zhuzi.
The Third Watch. The Sun-Cart of Jambudvīpa at Noon (卓船).
*The Recorded Sayings of Master Qiāoyǐn*, Volume One;
*The Recorded Sayings of Master Qiāoyǐn*, Volume Two.
The Dharma-speech was sent to the Lamp-Store Abbot Shen Guang,
who stole a single spark from the patriarch’s direct transmission and planted it amidst the pure, cold, and severe frost; with but a single arm...
Holding up the cold, they could not extinguish it. It was transmitted three times to Yuxin Mannaoliao, and four times to Longtan Deshan;
though they wished to quench its violent flames, from beginning to end they could not blow them out. At midnight on Mount Ao, the fire was gathered and the loot divided;
fifteen hundred men raked through the ashes and stirred the embers, lamp after lamp continuing the light as the radiance was distributed throughout the four seas. Even if—
Even if one were to pour forth the waters of the Flower Treasury Ocean and reverse the currents of the Jade Gorge, they would likely find it difficult to dampen his flame of wisdom.

Master Deng of the Lamp Repository came from the presence of the late Master Yuejian of Kaixian; he followed him at Xue Temple, where I frequently observed his refined character and dignified bearing, and how his spiritual resonance was transcendent.
One can truly know that, like the precipitous cliffs and strange rocks of Mount Lu, there are no ordinary plants or trees to be found there.

Winter of the Wushen year. After being troubled by my duties as Director of the Guizang (Repository of the Hidden), and having resigned from office, I suddenly felt nostalgia for my former seclusion and went to comfort the monkeys and cranes.

They presented me with paper requesting words to serve as companions for my journey; thus, I responded to them, saying: "Now, at the end of autumn in the Patriarchal Hall, the garden of awakening is cold as spring.
Amidst the weariness of battle and the intoxication of darkness, amidst the winds of fame and rains of profit, I vow to mold empty space into a single lamp-bowl and drain the nine..."
I take the Yangtze River as a single lamp-stand and the Five Elders Peak as a single lamp-wick, so that the three lamps of Shaolin, Longtan, and Xueqiao may shine brightly and inexhaustibly.
I shall stir the waves of the cold spring to wash my aging eyes, so that I may behold their magnificent radiance.
Go forth and exert yourself!
Attendant Deshōu returns to his hometown to visit his mother.
The misty waves of over thirty thousand *qīng* of Lake Tàihú exist in Sūzhōu; the purple and green of the seventy-two peaks of Dōngtíng do not exist elsewhere in the world.
Crows cry and the moon sets; the bell tolls in Cold Mountain. The traveler’s journey is still long; the sword’s light shines upon the empty pool.

The frost is cold upon the pulley; ancient regrets are difficult to erase. The spring in the gardens of Wu is thick; the fragrant heart has not yet ceased. The waters of the Yue River are swift; the misty boat is hard to find.
If you understand this as a description of a scene, you do not yet possess the eye of a traveling monk. If you do not understand it as a description of a scene, [you have it].
It was not that he lacked the eyes of a traveling mendicant; it was simply that he had not yet seen Xuefeng’s Way.

To take up the entire earth and reduce it to the size of a single grain of millet—here there is no place for you to move, and no place for you to choose. One must sweep away all objective conditions and shatter all barriers;
only those of outstanding brilliance and refined spirit can achieve this. Attendant Deshou was originally from the region of Wu.
Liye served at Cui Peak and came from afar to rely upon me at Xue Temple. Every time I saw him, he was grave, silent, and upright, diligently devoted to the Way.

I requested that he return to attend to the incense hall for one year. Master Gong’s courtesy name was Rijin; regarding his studies, once he had relinquished his official post, I intended to entrust him with the keys to the library.

Furthermore, I said: "Your mother is elderly and resides in the hall; as the times are currently plagued by famine and scarcity, we have not yet entered the summer retreat. You must remain to serve your mother."
The days are short; the days spent serving one's teacher are long. I beg for a word to serve as a warning and encouragement for my journey.
In the past, Prince Nanda returned his flesh, yet his filial piety was deficient; Master Muzhou wove reeds to offer service, yet his righteousness emerged from a year of abundance.

If you can capture the two Buddhas and the Patriarch in their state of mental exertion within a single phrase, then the mountains of Wu and the waters of Chu will not be removed from before your eyes;

the affection between mother and child will grow ever closer as it seems to distance itself. Only then will you know that the old man on the mountain head possesses a most profound and compassionate heart.

The attendant Shiyi was shown the upward path that not even a thousand sages have transmitted; the upward path is such that not even a thousand sages have realized it. Before a word is spoken, the Way is cut off.
A drop of water gives rise to ice; the thread of the path is let go. The double barrier stands like a cliff.
For students of the present day, to have doubts regarding all words and phrases is a great sickness; yet to have no doubts regarding all words and phrases is likewise a great sickness.
The oceanic roc spreads its wings; the celestial horse pursues the wind. A lion bites a man; a wild donkey chases after clods of earth. By the time you blink your eyes, you have already missed it.
Furthermore, there was another oversight. A monk named Sifu, a disciple of Yiming, had come from afar to rely upon [the Master]. He was asked to return to the attendants' quarters.
Whenever [the Master] saw him diligently pursuing the Way and maintaining his composure in silence, after the monk’s term of office ended, he burned incense and requested words for self-exhortation.
Thereupon, [the Master] said to him: "In the Hall of Preserved Fragrance, bowing to the seat and burning incense—is this speech? Or is it non-speech? (Three times.)
In the ball court, welcoming guests and seeing them off—is this a phrase? Is it a non-phrase?

Here, if you can see that the National Teacher never actually called out three times, and the attendant never actually responded three times, then it is either your fault toward me, or my fault toward you;
the innermost hearts of each are cast from forged iron.

The scene of his departure from the mountains is buffeted by winds of confusion and foul dust. Amidst the mistaken congealing of craving, he enters the golden womb. Having already scaled the city walls, it is too late to bite one's own navel;
though he dies of cold and hunger, his mind is difficult to turn back. "Departing the mountains, departing the mountains—what has he accomplished? To recognize even a single star is to be caught."
A star has gone astray; the river of Chan and the ocean of teaching cannot be swept dry. Turning back toward Handan, there are many mistaken paths.

At midnight, he leaped over the city wall with an iron heart and liver. Once the arrow has slipped from the empty string, it is difficult to pull it back by force. If there is a Way, one can succeed; even a mountain can be exited.
Yet, snow and frost still lack the cold of six years.

Avalokiteśvara’s wheel of vows silently operates through the true mechanism; the six sense-bases function interchangeably, all attaining spiritual penetration. The eight consciousnesses govern the vast emptiness where form and non-form coincide;

ten thousand phenomena clamor and strike, yet sound is not red. Fragrance wafts from lotuses; the frosty moon is bitter. With a compassionate heart, he acts specifically for the sake of people of this age.
Tilting. A single rain from the willow-flask levels the ocean of benefit. The murky waves dare not idly waft their stench. Returning the hearing, pure contemplation possesses great compassion;
in every realm of transformation, the capacities of beings are met with perfect penetration. Fragrance floats upon the golden lotuses as the green of the grasses turns azure;
numinous birds soar and gather as the celestial clouds lower. The Panṭa stone is cold while the tide beats against it; the willows by the jade flask are supple in spring.

Branch after branch, they seek me through sound like a shadow in the void; with their eyes, they see me through form as eyebrows in the center of the gaze. When will the youth of the hundred cities return?
With a weary heart, he pursues me afar as I fly upon the great waves.
Transcending and realizing perfect penetration, one suddenly forgets both light and its objects. The golden grasses are cold in color; the azure sky makes the spring day long.
With the eyes of meditative concentration unmoving, the willow by the vase is still.
In deep stillness, the long-standing rock returns with the night waves; A brocade heart and embroidered mouth open toward people.
Within a single needle’s eye, the three thousand worlds lie; The path has no gate—how joyful is Sudhana!

(Quoting embroidery) Golden sand cannot hide the jade soul as it flies; The fragrance of the green lotus fades, and awakening from the dream is slow. One should attain [enlightenment] through the body of a bhikṣu.
[The Buddha] has passed away. Skull, wait until your eyes open! (Golden Sand: Manifests as an old monk carrying a skull.

Maitreya (sleeping while sitting) is greedily attached to the mundane world; he does not dwell in his exalted status. Piling up his body as he sits on the ground, whom is he waiting for? Throughout the entire world, who is there?
Of the same kind. Within this realm of deficiency and decay, wind and waves daily increase. With eyes closed as before, one cannot sleep.
Having abandoned Tuṣita Heaven and descended into the world of Jambudvīpa, though you hold the master’s staff upon your shoulder, you have not yet escaped losing the cloth bag.
There is not a single thing for sale; buying high and selling low, the mountain colors of Changting are as green as dark eyebrows.
There is no need for haste regarding the goods within the bag; the waters wind around the marsh, their currents long and winding.
Who would believe that in the brief moment of stretching beneath the pine, the Tuṣita Palace has already been shrouded in several shades of twilight? (Stretching beneath the pine).

Bodhidharma crossed the reed-flowing sands; the celestial gates were neither barred nor bolted. An old man, harboring theft and deceit, peered into the royal court. The jade steps of the palace are strictly guarded by nine tigers;
his vermilion face is ashamed to reflect against the light red robes. In Chang’an, O Chang’an, the sound of rain and snow falls; the wind through the reeds shakes leaf after leaf.
My heart’s banner is deeply moved by the waters at the head of the Yangtze River; not a single wave can wash away the stench of dust and filth.

Auspicious mists rise over the Tai City as the royal aura renews; how could the dust of barbarian hordes defile the springtime of the Jade Tower? Of the hundred thousand who have come from the West, none possess a true foundation;
among them, not half a person is fully capable of taking up this burden.

A single word against the scales of a dragon’s neck: even four horses cannot overtake the tongue. A single reed against a contrary current: the retreating waves do not turn back. In Loyang, the dream of a military expedition was drenched in wind and snow;
at the Phoenix Terrace, one leans against the void as it towers desolately in the sky.
The Treasure Master manifested wonders and gathered spiritual essence; his path was like drifting clouds and soaring birds. His twelve faces could not be painted by the monk Zhaoyi;
his thirty-six transformations could not be fathomed by King Liang. Palace ladies attend him with their jade hairpins lowered; celestial deities guard him with golden locks clasped.
The eagle’s nest: the moon is cold. The crane’s pagoda: the wind is high. The events of over nine hundred years remain vividly present.
Deep mountains, warm clouds, and ancient, weathered pines.
The Fish Basket Guanyin.
The jewel within the robe reveals its brilliance; the fish basket emits a wind of stench. She flaunts her female beauty, using the false to confound the true.
One truly knows that leaning against the market cannot topple a city.

Her hair is disheveled and her hairpins askew, yet her bearing is elegant and refined; she stands with hands folded, silent. Playing with the real as if it were the false, she finally sets down the fish basket.
What was it like at that time? He set down the price of the land (placing the basket upon the ground).

Dīpaṃkara received him upon his head; his sleeves were as magnificent as clouds. He trailed his staff; his monastic robes were light and pure. When he encountered the tyranny of the times, the flies...

A fragment of jade was born. To exhort the wicked toward goodness, his person became a fortress of Dharma; with the radiance of tranquil concentration, he was like the bright moon in the midst of heaven.
His ocean of vows was boundless, as the tides of the hundred rivers settled into peace. Responding to conditions through resonance, he manifested as rain or as sun.
These were but a single mote of dust within the Master’s power of aspiration. The Great Void is vast and empty; to apply brush and ink there would be in vain.
Hanshan carries a broken bamboo tube in his hand; what a leisurely manner! Scattered and sparse, he has discarded a few scraps of vegetables.
Joyfully and cheerfully, they meet and boast of the flavor of their stew. Its fragrance permeates the pores of Samantabhadra.
The brush is set aside in silent contemplation; within my mind there is no "living phrase. My pure bones are as thin as withered wood, for I have suffered much from the toil of composing poetry.
Upon the leaves of the banana tree, there is no rain of sorrow. (On a Poem Inscribed on a Banana Leaf)
Shide sweeps the thatched grass; with a single flavor he plays with the strange and marvelous. Flying and fluttering in profusion, he sweeps ceaselessly all day long.
Shivering and whistling, the wind from the pine treetops sounds through the pipes. The golden world of Mañjuśrī lies in utter disarray.
Mistakenly setting foot upon the cold crags, my dreams follow the whirl of the dusty world. Leaning on my staff, I contemplate in silence; the traveler’s heart is filled with lingering attachment.
The road back to Mount Emei is as vast as the heavens.
The First Patriarch trod through the heat and trampled the cold, crossing sands and deserts. At the Phoenix Terrace, the spring mist is deep; at the Heron Marsh, the cold tide ebbs.
The palace of the Liang dynasty could not tolerate such obscurity; Master Baozhi vainly attempted to sketch it. Shen Guang’s single hand ultimately could not support it—Mount Song.
From youth until now, my coldness has been severe and my countenance foul.

The Second Patriarch sought the Way with great hardship; his cultivation lacked power, his waist was deeply burdened by accumulated resentment, and while his skin was as white as snow, his heart remained stained. He severed but a single [limb].

What peace can the arm find in the heart? To perform three prostrations and receive [the Dharma]—what delusion is this! Having suddenly obtained spring from within the sleeve, the flowers and fruits of Shaolin have lost their color.
The third patriarch’s past karma permeated his very skin; his entire body was illness. Seeking the source of his transgressions, he found no root; this was a true illness difficult to cure.

Having failed to shed the worldly airs of a layman, he lured Sima Hong into a dark pit. As it passed through three transmissions, the flowers and leaves spread their fragrance ever more widely, becoming like a wolf—[preying upon the ignorant].
Relying on what can one endure the spring filling the paths?

At the Fourth Patriarch’s Rock, solitary Chan is fixed. Without being sealed by the "pillow under the ribs," liberation has no gate. Opening one's eyes, one enters a false concentration; this is called the Great [Delusion].
The physician revives the dead with no fixed method; he deceives the dhūta, reversing the natural course of his aged life. The purple clouds dissipate and the flowers and birds perish;
the wind shakes Mount Niu-tou as the rain clears away.

The Fifth Patriarch, at the end of his journey as evening fell, took a wrong turn and entered a womb. He defiled the muddy waters of the harbor; though he swam against the current and nearly drowned, he did not die.

His verse inscribed on the wall confused and deluded the assembly of seekers. Uncovering the thief’s loot, he led people across in secret. From this time on, the monastic communities were left with a lingering air of poverty and hardship. Huai...
The mountain broods as it listens to the Huangmei rains.

The Sixth Patriarch’s transmission of the Dharma was without artifice; though he possessed the strength to carry firewood, he concealed himself in a dilapidated mortar house. He inscribed a verse upon the wall of the *Laṅkāvatāra* Sūtra and stole the robe, staining it with filth.

Yun: He associated with hunters; his arguments on the wind and the banner were flawed, and his own person lacked secrecy. His ill repute lasts for a thousand ages, bringing shame upon the ancestral tradition.
Yet, in eighty lifetimes, he served as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Zheng Huangniu’s shoulders rise and fall as he strides; his fixed gaze is as still as Lake Hu. Huangniu’s horns point toward heaven, while eight legs hang down past his nose.
Beyond the words, one must clarify this very meaning.

Master Yushan turns his head to look at the blue sky; he pays no heed at all to what is beneath his feet. He stumbles and falls, his eyes dizzy with floating flowers. Mountains and rivers shine their light through the night.
A horn has grown upon the head of the lame donkey.

Master Xiǎnzì used shrimp as his eyes to look toward people; though he dredged the river waves until they were empty, his heart remained unextinguished. A monk who does not uphold the precepts—how can one blame him?
It is because he has come forth from within the temple.
The Pig-Headed Monk is thoroughly worldly and utterly foolish; he directly presents the opening of the "dead eye. His mouth has never known the taste of flavor;
the Pig-Head eats his fill while observing the pure fast.

One who takes the Way as their principle—how could they ever have awakened to the profound meaning of the Patriarchs? On the traveler’s road through Tongcheng, wind and mist stretch far and wide. The *kāṣāya* robe has no form;
the sandals have no thread. With such tattered seams, it can never fully wrap one about.

The ancient strategy of Master Quan Daodao rests across his shoulder, its resonance transcending the mundane dust. Before one’s eyes, the Great Way manifests its complete reality. Within the ladle, every beat of the rhythm is like an ocean of spring;
a single drop is enough to intoxicate all who encounter it.
Master Hōjō and I met on the road;
we sought a truthful discussion. What need was there for your words, sister, or his words, Master?
With the spring rains turning everything to fresh green, the scars upon the ox’s back are difficult to wash away.

Yantou’s single stroke of the oar—like a thundering snowfall—is not easily requited. The beloved child was cast away; the grief is difficult to contain. The waves of grace lap against the shore where no path exists;
the moon is full over Lake Dongting in autumn.

Zhaozhou (holding his rosary) saw that the people of Yan and Zhao were arrogant and conceited; he did not descend from his meditation seat to meet Nanquan, for had he attempted to engage him directly, he would have erred.

An obstruction remained within him, and more than seven hundred years of the sexagenary cycle passed in vain. With this single string of beads, he never transcended non-virtue, even though many years had elapsed.
The Ancient Buddha Zhaozhou:
Touzi (carrying an oil lamp) visited Cuiwei to inquire about the meaning of the West;
Zhaozhou confronted him as "inviting a thief to ruin the house," presenting the truth directly before one's face and leading the ghost [to its destination].
Entering for the funeral rites: from the moment of first seeing [the truth], one is entirely deluded; in its actual application, how could there ever be any core?
Have you not heard the words of Touzi?
"Planting pine trees."
The nascent mind cannot let go. A white-haired old dhūta. Before a single inch has entered the earth, the branches already obstructing others are many.
How can one endure the words of those who come to buy firewood? The village barbarians emerge from Lingnan; they do not recognize a single character. Yet the firewood in their hands is ready at once.
Carrying it.
Wuzu looked at Yuanwu (The Diagram of the Rooster Flying onto the Balustrade):

The water is cold, the bridge spans across; the mountains are deep, the clouds are warm. Pointing east while speaking of the west, thoughts and emotions are in turmoil. Startled awake by the sound of roosters.
Sentiments for one’s Hometown. At Jiange Pass there is no ladder; my dreams of returning are severed.
Bazhang attended Mazu (Painting of Wild Ducks seen while traveling by mountain):

The shadows of the marsh birds flutter gracefully. They fly and gather, each finding its own kind. The traveler’s nose grows sour with grief. In this place of pain, who can I rely upon to entrust my sorrows?
The reflection of the towers and terraces reveals the mountain’s countenance; solitary clouds do not fly as heaven rests upon the water.

On the level fields, travelers meet on their paths; they speak in rustic dialects. When the ox’s back aches, the whip is applied once more—mostly for the sake of what is uneven, yet with a single plow, [the field is leveled].
The spring rain makes the high plateau deep; to this day, the paths of the level fields have been overgrown with weeds.

Striking the horn, one contemplates the autumn gloom of India; the flying bird arrives under the moonlit night. In equal measure, they toy with their own spirits; life and death are difficult to relinquish. Upon the ox’s back...
Striking the *jiao* note amidst the sounds, its lingering resonance drifts afar beneath the tall pines.
Baizhang’s single shout deafened the ears; mountains crumbled and oceans tilted. It is as if he were walking while speaking—vivid as the sun and stars, using his very body as his tongue.
To correct the errors of the present age and take oneself as the standard, one remains ever new across a hundred generations.

While the vast currents of later times are like the war of ants and birds, beholding these remaining images, the obscured mind should become clear. Like the ancient trees of one’s homeland, they still preserve the traces of the ancestral laws.
The founding patriarch, Zen Master Jingjue, was already deceived by Deqiao when he struck him off with his staff; leaping down from the guest bed, he was secretly set aside by Yantou.
These twelve people were the first to join the covenant; they were not material for great pillars. These fifteen hundred followers were gathered from the very head of the village;
they were likewise not vessels of jade and pearl. When a monk raises the teaching to its ultimate height, there is, in truth, no handle to grasp.
It would not be a mistake to call them the local deities of Seven Villages.

The stele inscription for Master Yuan: At Wuguan in Yanmen, the mountain peaks are clear after the rain; at Tiger Creek, the turbulent rapids grind against the teeth of the stones. The society of Donglin is cold and the night watches are long;
white lotus flowers bloom amidst a fine mist of fragrance. The elegance of the Jin era has faded with its robes and caps; the sound of the Great Odes has sunk into a deep silence.
The tiles are the monument; empty space is the paper; the old events of the portrait hall are difficult to record.

The hat on the crag is heavy, the raincoat is light; the command is strict, yet the Dharma has fallen into decay. When the oars are set down and one stands waiting in thought, the boatman has not yet arrived. How desolate!
Regretfully following the wind that stirs the duckweed, the boatman’s three-inch hook has been cast;
his life hangs by a single thread. Though he is clever, no one comes; Daowu remains silent, with no news at all. — Zhu Ya.
The tides recede and the cold redness falls silent.

The Girl of Spiritual Insight sells out all traces of her poor-woman’s appearance; it is mostly because she resents her father. Her money from the winnowing-fan is full to the farthing; she allows cash payment, but not credit.

A single handful of lotus fragrance from the Horse-herd Maiden floats up; she entices people with the hook of desire. The golden sand marks and jade-like coldness cannot conceal the Horse-herd Maiden’s shame.
The Fish Basket (Dana holds up his staff).
A single point of compassionate heart extends as far as the heavens and the sea. Half-draped in pearl robes, they cast a cold radiance. They flaunt these marks of poverty and lowliness;
the fishy stench of their basket stains the fragrance of the jade lotus.

His robes were worn thin with cold, his patched cassock chilled; his countenance was ancient and his spirit lofty. He was a steadfast companion to the lean old man Pang, facing Lingzhao face-to-face amidst the clash of weapons.
"Is the Layman here? Is the Layman here? With a three-foot staff, he stirs the Yellow River.
The morning sun breaks through, leaving no part of the body unexposed; in vain do they attempt to measure it with the blade and ruler. When the effort is dense and subtle, one must act with urgency;
for the cold days have not yet gained even a single thread’s length.

Facing the moon in leisurely idleness, who is busy with fruits and beans? Snow covers the brows of the pair of eyes, gazing upon the frost. The sutras are difficult to exhaust, their meanings hard to fathom;
how many times have the moons grown dim at the roots of the clouds?

At the Tōrinsha Shrine in Misaki, the warmth of spring lingers; white lotuses waft their fragrance. Those who uphold the precepts and those who break them have not yet forgotten their attachment to outward forms. How can the sound of the mountain stream compare to the length of laughter?

Four sleeping men with tigers for companions—what kind of fire-partners are these? Their hearts and faces differ; dreams and visions are in turmoil. The wind shakes the pine gate as spring colors fade at evening.
Postscript to the Inscription by Master Chijue on the Heart Sutra (Following the Inscriptions of Various Elders):

The Prajñāpāramitā heart-dharma discussed by the Venerable of the Spirit Mountain (Śākyamuni) in the sutra has not yet been exhausted; it is now transmitted upon this paper by the Venerable of the Great White (Chijue).
The methods of Prajñā have not yet been exhausted; the various elders praised them within their discourse. Yet, as for the phrasing of Prajñā, Xuefeng’s way of speaking has not reached it.
To speak thus, he cannot avoid incurring the sin of slandering Prajñā.
An Inscription on a Painting of a Chan Assembly:
From the Han to the Tang dynasties, the Buddha-dharma was as brilliantly manifest as the sun at the zenith of the sky. At that time, sovereigns were sagacious and awaited sages;

their treatment of teachers was generous and profound. Many bathed their eyes in the river of Chan and tasted the flavor of the Dharma, leaving their names recorded in abundance upon bamboo and silk—such was the case with Pang [Zong].
