The lineage of the Elder: sitting, standing, laughing, and conversing; playing within birth and death—this was sufficient to rouse and inspire a degenerate age. Alas! The mountains and rivers are silent and desolate;

the eras have faded away. The cliffs are withered and the waters have receded; the claws are hidden and the scales have vanished. It is not only that I feel shame when meeting those of the present time.
I am likewise ashamed to behold this painting.

That the Arhats crossing the water are depicted as having been dispersed into vessels represents the dilution of the Way; that they have adapted to change represents the decay of the Dharma. Behold these sixteen [Arhats]!
The Bodhisattvas travel through space like clouds and tread upon water as if on land. Dragons soar and tigers crouch;
lions spring and elephants wheel about. Cranes cry and monkeys shriek; there are deer, flowers, and monkey fruits.

Reflecting upon that time, it was not far from the stage of the Great Vehicle, yet they delighted in supernatural powers as mere childish play and trivial matters. Alas! The dilution of the Way and the decay of the Dharma can be observed therein.
Inscription on the Calligraphic Manuscript of Master Fuxin, Presented to Archivist Yuan.

In ancient times, Zhang Liang obtained the *Sushu* (Book of White) bestowed by Master Shi. Liang was able to employ even a mere fraction of its essential principles—its dregs were sufficient to destroy Qin and establish Han.
Now, I have transmitted this *Pushe* (General Discourse) written by my late teacher, Master Fuxin, to my nephew, Archivist Deyuan.
My Lord, if you can put what he has said into practice, then the entire land will look to you as the legacy of your father’s and grandfather’s calling;
that you can perpetuate their family tradition—how could this be something desired by you alone, any less than by Zhang Liang?
After the scroll of poems on mountain dwelling by Master Baiyun, Chijue Heshang wrote:
"The clouds within Mount Baiyun possess a subtle stillness amidst their idleness; the clouds within Yushan Hermitage possess an idleness amidst their subtlety."
As for Yu Long, his emergence from seclusion and his subsequent withdrawal differed in timing, yet the essence of his tranquil detachment remained one and the same.
Alas! Worldly affairs are but fleeting vanity; the decaying tide flows on daily. Like white clouds turning into blue dogs, all changes in an instant.
When shall I bind my thatched hut beneath the long pines, gaze upon the poems of this elder, and continue his rhyme to fulfill my humble aspirations? Having happened to read this scroll, it truly...
He captured my heart.

The calligraphy for the "Seven Households Village" plaque by the monk Tong of Xuankong was written on the back of a scroll from Yanshan in Liyang—a place that serves as a lodging for travelers throughout the world.
Since the time of the local deity of Seven Households Village, the families have been decimated and the households ruined; they rely upon...
After the depletion of wealth and resources, more than four hundred years passed; those who wished to receive a single plot of land to become commoners were few and far between.
A mountain man from Xuánfēng labored at the pen to earn his livelihood, securing half a *dǔ* of land to fulfill his ambition for a secluded retreat among hills and gardens.

Where the cocks crow and dogs bark, the sounds reach across the four borders; they vied with one another to offer congratulations, yet still desired a humble word from this rustic to follow after them. Thus—
It is said: "The family is poor, yet they wish for a wealthy neighbor.
Inscribed on the *Sāṃsārika-citra*:
"Spring sunshine over washed brocade; night rain upon the reed window. When one smiles beneath the thatched eaves, where is the world of Śākya? The three lives..."

Separation from what one loves; a kind of encounter with the hated and reviled. Waves strike the boat as the painted scroll is unfurled; the wind carries horses and oxen afar while the Gutang Gorge rages.
At the request of Master Longzang, I inscribe this colophon after the writings of Dahui.
I solemnly examine the handkerchief of the Elder Miaoxi and Master Xing’an. It begins by saying: "He employs the bamboo staff without a moment’s rest; he is concerned for the Way.
Having found capable men in both places, the common people are most fortunate; this brings joy to the state.
How could those of later generations who disparage the Buddhists—claiming they lack the way of loyalty and filial piety—possibly be right? — Recorded by Dharma Master Longzang.
I hope that through these means, we may honor our Way and stabilize those who are frivolous and shallow.
Regarding the original calligraphy of "Aoshan Ge" (Turtle Mountain Pavilion) by Master Yongzhai Zhao:
the Master inscribed the three characters "Aoshan Ge" in large script to serve as a plaque for the reception hall at Zhongji, welcoming those who come from afar.
A man of such caliber, who knows the warning of the overturned carriage, how could he have no concern for his future lives?

The monk Jing of Chaoyang brought forth this portrait, and the venerable elders of all quarters vied with one another to provide inscriptions and colophons. Desiring to add a single word to its conclusion, I said to him:
"The present age is but a guest-house of great peace; your Zen staff has grown weary of wandering. Who now would dream of the Mount Ao of immortals?"
This scroll should be bound away on a high shelf.
Regarding the postscript to the letter by Sima Wen Gong:

when I was a child, I read his writings; his rectification of the ruler and his benefit to the people, his promotion and demotion, and his administration of advancement and dismissal were such that even the likes of Dong Hu and Shi Chou could not have surpassed them.
He was able to surpass them. His mother was Lady Nie, the Grand Dowager of Wengu. I am humbled to share the same clan with her.

I did not expect that more than two hundred and fifty years after his passing, I would still be able to behold his own handiwork. The phrasing therein is upright and meticulous, while the force of his brushwork is vigorous and powerful;
its brilliance is cold and its color pure, so solemn and imposing as to be inviolable. It is as if I were suddenly beholding Confucius within the "Xiangdang" chapter.
The Wen *vina* requested a title for the late master Foxin Shitian’s practice at Xixi.
To the north of the mountain, amidst precipitous cliffs and sheer walls, there lies a plot of land that no one has ever truly beheld with the right eye.
Master Chen took his three-inch bald brush and turned it over entirely, transmitting it with bare hands. How extraordinary!
This was my former karma. Since then, I have plowed deeply but sown shallowly; I cook rice-less porridge and feed myself to satiety before others arrive.
When the Venerable Wen, the *karmadāna*, produced an old promissory note and wished for me to act as a guarantor with full clarity, I rolled it up and returned it to him, saying:
"The pattern is not found here."
The Abbot Su Sang requested a preface for the frontispiece of his volume.
The Abbot Su Sang of the Immortal School had cleared a meditation hall and inscribed it with his own name, "Su Sang," and requested that I certify its meaning.

I therefore said to him: "In these times, the winds of fame and the rains of profit blow fiercely; the world is intoxicated by the fray of strife. The net of attachment and the river of emotion ensnare all, as people drown in their greed."
Jun: For example, it is like a lost person traveling through a vast wilderness at night who does not strike the ground to find a place to stay, yet seeks to escape the shackles of the world.
It is not easily attained. Our Buddha, the founder of the Tathāgata school, established the precept that one should not stay under a tree for more than three nights.
The world has sometimes criticized this, claiming it lacks the righteousness of human relations and seeks self-extinction through severance.

Yet they fail to realize that true practice leaves no trace, true emptiness has no dependence, true illumination has no object, and true dreaming has no awakening. Heaven and earth are but a straw hut; the three realms are a mere reversal.
On a journey, even insects, plants, and trees are all my kin; where, then, could one not find a place to lodge?
If, however, one’s thoughts do not cease and one’s state does not remain constant from moment to moment, then with every step raised and every step taken, where would not be beneath the *sāla* tree?
Supplementary Record on the Southern Route Fire-Tent (followed by ten verses for bowing to the Patriarchs).
Master Xuanzi brought forth the Southern Route Fire-Tent from his sleeve; I rubbed my aging eyes and examined it thoroughly.
Among its contents, there were ten items listed in hand-written notes, each clearly detailed. However, it was improper to take items belonging to the monastery that had been held for many years.
To take these for one’s own use constitutes an infringement that fails to preserve integrity. My original intention was to include the wooden chair (mokujō) from the same set;
however, as I have been occupied with basking in the sun, I lack the leisure to do so now. For the time being, I shall simply record this on the brush.
Later, I shall carve a notice upon the Unnamed Stele to inform all and serve as a warning to those who might later encroach upon the mountain’s resources.
Eulogy for the Librarian Bafu (His Posthumous Name: Anxi; He Was My Junior Disciple): The window plum crosses the snow;
the eaves bamboo brightens the frost. All sounds have subsided into silence; the true melody has fallen into desolation.

Just as I was in a state of sudden "sitting-forgetfulness," the Librarian Tieshan arrived at my door and presented a large scroll. It was a eulogy for a renowned figure of the mountains, written by his nephew.
The Assistant Archivist offered words of condolence; unconsciously, my aged heart was moved by a sense of melancholy.
I then wiped the moss-covered stone and, beyond the strings of a lute, once again pressed my fingers to play. The clouds on the banks grew somber at dusk, and the western sun sank into the shadows.
What tune could this possibly be? It is like the Master weeping for Yan Hui.
A Letter from Master Miaoxi to Grand Master Miaokong:

The virtue and conduct of our predecessors were full and abundant, their fragrance spreading in all directions. Even in an age a hundred generations hence, though the texts may be incomplete and the scrolls fragmented, those who obtain them regard them as no less than the "night-glittering" gem or the "Bian" jade.
Yet, with the decline of customs and the thinning of integrity, people have abandoned the substantial for the ornamental; thus, the Way has not reached its former heights.
Though it may overflow its borders, with flowers as brilliant as brocade, it does not last more than the blink of an eye before being cast aside against the walls;

it is truly worse than mere chaff and weeds. Now, observing the Elder Miaoxi, he has accepted the Governor’s invitation and responded to Miaokong’s letter, borrowing his *tusuo* (New Year’s wine) for a brief stay while traveling.
He attends to every detail of firewood and fuel, fearing only that a single thought might arise. His...

His pure virtue and meticulous conduct were such that he almost feared others would know of them; one cannot fathom how it was that his mouth, which at that time uttered such unrestrained blasphemies against Heaven, could have escaped the taboos of the age.
Alas! "While they lived there were people; when they died there were books. Having happened upon this letter, my thoughts toward his lofty character and noble conduct are redoubled.
When those great men of the past employed the pivot of their great capacity—be it by picking up a flower and smiling, or by severing an arm to settle the mind—the Dharma was already in decline.

Yet they further employed the striking of staffs and the shouting of "Ho," setting up arrows and brandishing spears, claiming they had attained the great capacity and great function. They were utterly unaware that this was like the discharge of a powerful crossbow bolt when its strength is spent.
In the end, he was unable to pierce even thin silk. The Master used the term "Great Function" (*dàjī*) as his own title, and each of the eminent monks offered words to provoke it;
the essential meaning of that Great Function and Great Utility is entirely contained therein. Being humble and rustic, I dare not add a single word after this.
Have you not seen what was at the bottom of Xuefeng?
The Master Quan uses the scale to weigh the lightness or heaviness of objects;
nothing but a steelyard can bring them to equilibrium. As for the gravity or lightness of the Dharma, none but a Perfected Man can bear it.
This Master Quan uses "the balance" as his own title; this is because he wishes to uphold his own sense of unevenness.
While the various masters have vied with one another to settle the matter without a hair’s breadth of error, he still desires a word from this mountain monk to correct its conclusion.
It can hardly be avoided that we must once again mark the mountains where no stars appear: one, two, three, four; four, three, two, one.

In the *Huayan Zhizhang Tu* (Diagram of the Avatamsaka at the Fingers and Palms), it is stated that the Dharma-realm of the Avatamsaka encompasses the ten voids. Those who are deluded regarding its fundamental principle turn their backs on awakening and unite with sensory dust; those who lose its essential intent...

Turning southward or heading north, there are often those who cannot avoid the lament of Yang Zhu weeping at the fork in the road. The Elder of the Bamboo Courtyard has synthesized and summarized these teachings;

he inscribed them on the books of Sangzi and published them, so that everyone may, with a single lift of the head, find the seven locations and nine assemblies before their eyes, and with a single gathering of thought, perceive the winds and moonlight of a hundred cities as if pointing at one’s own palm. Should one, however, cling to appearances...
Seeking [him], I painted this upon the spring breeze while the greenery still persists.
A verse following the lament for Master Zhongshan of the Secluded Rock, composed in the spring of the *bichen* year of the Yuanyou era.
In the autumn of the *wumao* year of Yuanyou, I raised up Zhongshan; in the autumn of the same year, I wept for Zhongshan. One joy.
A single, profound lament. Without cause, without cause. Kāśyapa, in vain longing, calls out to Ānanda.
"In mourning for my son," [this concludes] the *Xuantong Shuji* (Record of Profound Penetration), Volume [X]. (The Record of Xuefeng, the Secretary of Xichan, while residing at Lingshi Yuan.

The auspicious phoenix emerges from the crimson valley; the written classics comprise the *Liubao*. Among the seven households of the village, the righteous army nurtures its sharp edge. Once the demons have been completely swept away.
The Crane-Releasing Pavilion is empty; he died guarding the profound pivot. Ten thousand men could not pull it out. "The deceased Zhuge can put the living Zhongda to flight.
[This refers to] the verse following the funeral banner for the Head Seat Wanshan Yi:
"The world was burned to emptiness; empty space cannot burn emptiness" (these two lines are from Ci-guo’s eulogy). The Elder of Quiescent Extinction. Truly.
One wishes to burn away the karmic offenses of the mouth committed during one's lifetime and to scrub clean the stains upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

yet little do they realize that the slander following death will cause the fierce flames of torment to blaze even more intensely. Xuefeng, seeing this injustice, acted with righteous courage, yet he could not avoid having to repent for it once again.
*Du!* Leap out of the fire pit and the ten-thousand-fathom-high mountain of blades!
Written by Xiaoweng, Huoshan, and Yunquan during the Duanping era of the Jiading period.
These three great masters—Xiaoweng, Huoshan, and Yunquan—possessed a reputation as formidable as thunder and lightning, shaking the ears of the deaf and the dull.
Two were renowned for the Way, and one was renowned for poetry. Even today, a thousand years later, though their works exist only as fragmentary manuscripts and broken scrolls...
Those who obtain it do so not merely as one finds a "night-glowing" gem or the "Bian" jade. Having recently perused these three scrolls, I was moved to three sighs.
Regarding the four inscriptions on the back of the scroll by the Head Seat of Shihu:
Shihu early on displayed a spirit of vigor and an ambition beyond the common herd. He journeyed far northward, traversing through both cold and heat across the imperial maps.

Its breadth is nearly half that [of the former]. It is a region where mountains and rivers manifest spiritual mysteries, and where Buddhas and patriarchs have left traces of their transformative teachings.

These things are visible before one’s eyes; how could it be limited to these four matters alone? In my view, this is what is meant by saying that when the people of Zan and Xi entered the Pass, they first secured the maps and records.

The Venerable Chen transcribed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations" and "Discernment of Vision through Eight Reversals" using his own blood. He exhorted and guided his young son, exhausting his verbal karma.

This was the Elder Gautama yielding to the sentiments of affection for his younger brother. The Venerable Chen of the Jiading era poured out the blood from his fingers and subsequently inscribed it with his brush. Thus it is.

To continue the Buddha’s life-force and ensure that the lineage remains unbroken—all depends on this. Let future worthies not fall into the error of Master An’s practice of breaking the lines of verse;
let them preserve the integrity of the scroll after the clouds have parted.

Vastly it unfurls and rolls up; brilliantly it is like ancient brocade. Divided into fragments and cut into pieces, sometimes severed and sometimes joined—this is seen within the verses arising amidst the clouds in the Cypress Courtyard.
It is but a single place, yet still lacking completeness. Let me try to supplement it for you from the Snowy Mountains.
Nail it down! Hang it up!
In these verses:

At the Treasure Master’s Stūpa, the murderous energy of the soaring hawk stirs the treetops; the Qin River reflects his image as the water-marks intertwine; the iron net that shrouds the heavens troubles my kerchief.
Below. Complete? Partially searching the old overturned nest.
The Stupa of Fayan (is located) in the vegetable garden of Wuxiang Monastery in Jiankang;
coming and going, the myriad functions are dark and still. It has long been a matter of adding mud to the wall; one has not yet finished the journey of their former travels.
A story: Inside and outside the fence, the vegetables have sprouted from their hearts.
Regarding the "Diamond Drill" story of Baoning’s Pagoda (located behind Tiesuo Temple at the South Gate of Jiankang), how can it be endured?
Its price demands the heavens; though dead, he has not yet accepted it. The Great Dharma-vehicle is a rope and an iron chain.
Ruined. One source: "Autumn colors lock the south of the city.
The Pagoda of Ying’an (at Tiantong):

"Once having passed through the tiger’s den, one nearly met the *chansha* [crabs]. To the end of death it is difficult to guard against their venomous claws and fangs; my bitter resentment remains buried to this day."
Attained. When the spring breeze blows the blood onto the peach blossoms, what gate of enlightenment has Mitan Daiche ever possessed?
As for his final words, what indeed did he follow? At that time, there was no grain left to be winnowed.
A single grain. Not reaching the end, one exhausts and burdens one's descendants.
Broken Hermitage Pagoda (located at Mount Jing):

the hermitage is ruined, the people are gone, and the weeds grow of their own accord. Among the family possessions, there is not a single thing that can be divided. A stupa three feet high reaches toward the heavens.
Below, the clouds atop Lingxiao Peak are obstructed and blocked;
at Shitian Pagoda, the three circumambulate the moss-covered grotto to voice their grievances. The wasteland remains uncultivated as few men till the soil. The spring breeze rewrites the covenant.
Jie: His family resided in Lihua Village and his surname was Peng.

At Wutai’s Fangshi, his power was vast and his wisdom great as he cleared the mysterious passageway. Golden light surged from his hair, and the stone ripples with a cold radiance. Seated at his desk, he managed ten thousand affairs without a single lapse.
To turn [the wheel of Dharma] is easy when following the ways of the world, but it is difficult for a person to achieve perfection.
At Mount Xiang, amidst the red earth, one carves into one's own bones;

how could one ever forget the profound kindness of one’s father? When the eyes are obscured by the waters of affection, even the heavens grow dark. With a heart of bitter resolve, one grinds away until all flying dust is exhausted.
The earth—its bloodstains from falling wounds are difficult for a thousand hands to gather.
At the White Horse Stele Terrace, the Way is vast and obscure;
one prizes the darkened mind. How could truth and falsehood allow even a single hair’s breadth of intrusion? Polluted blood does not follow the scorched soil.
Exhausted. The entanglements leave no shadow to obscure the gold.
At Shaolin, the shadow-stone dwells solitary and alone;
in the snow-chamber, it is in vain. For nine years there was no place to set a face of shame. Throughout his life, the missing features were finally revealed.
Ugly! Though the severed moss may shield the stone, the teeth remain cold.
Sending off the Abbot Jūn of Chánglú:

Heaven is desolate and earth is old; his realization transcends the ancestral lineage. As the setting sun and solitary clouds, eye meets eye in emptiness. The separate transmission outside the teachings leaves nothing remaining.
The Dharma: A cold reed-flute wind blows across the Long River.
Iron Hermit’s fist is raised, forged from pure steel; how many can withstand the blow and perceive its intent? It has not yet reached the vast, roaring furnace.
Cold. The embroidered flowers have eroded the traces of spring on the walls.

At Taiyuan, I heard that Old Mei Fu was mistakenly seeking fragrance within his dreams; though he saw it amidst the thicket of sounds and colors, he has not yet forgotten it. The seasonal breeze at the Twenty-four Bridges.
Far away, branch after branch blows forth resentment rather than fragrance.

A great blessing, the plum tree is exiled to a thicket of ten thousand plants where it alone monopolizes its splendor. Poets set aside their brushes, struggling in vain to describe it. Had it not been for its sparse blossoms amidst the malarial mists...
Without, who would believe that there is a distinct fragrance upon the branches?

To mourn the Master Xueyan of Yangshan, entangled in grief beneath the twin trees—how lamentable! To speak of the unspeakable is too much prolixity; the karmic winds stir coldly through Xueyan’s snow.
Snow. One night it buried little Śākyamuni.
In the autumn of the Gengyin year, my late teacher, Master Jue’an, passed away at Cēn Mountain in Hangzhou. Upon hearing the news of his demise, I composed this verse:
Clouds disperse from the peaks of Mount Cen as the moon hangs over autumn; the mountain stream wails mournfully as it flows day and night. A filial child should have come to inquire after him;
weeping for his master, tears fall upon the tips of his forehead.

In the secret chamber, single-mindedly hold up this one phrase: "The Iron Kunlun. Occupying the seat, all directions are shrouded in blinding daylight. How could it be fit for transmission in the dark?
Huangmei let the thief loose and opened the door himself.
The Chief Seat Guang has left his post to reside at Chongfu;
having already departed as chief seat, the auspicious colors of the mountain embrace the clear sky. He himself knows he has incurred great enmity;
it is no wonder he encounters those from Xuefeng who revile him.
Roaming through three ancient temples:

The wind lowers the jade grass; the dark tide wells up from the spring. Earth opened and Heaven revealed, revealing the primordial chaos (*hun-yuan*). One does not know this foundation was already there;
Only after three ascents and nine climbs did one enter another's gate.
The Manjusri Terrace rises coldly above the clouds, a single strand of azure hair; high above, a path divides the flying dust. A long rainbow pierces the sun as the mountain holds its reflection;
it bends to form a golden arm extended for one.

The spring flows and recedes in accordance with the tides, its trustworthiness unswerving; the stone basin holds a limpid azure that naturally forms clear ripples. Mountain flowers, having shed the rain, float with glossy crimson;
their fragrance permeates the Tailgate (Weilu), yet spring remains unknowing.

Friends conversing at night, as the chilling wind whistles through the window curtains. Sitting still in silent discourse, the crescent moon slants across the gap. A single word in a contest of wit loses the subtle turn;
across the bed, flying spittle drenches the lamp-flower.
Master Quan has returned to his home in Jianye, dwelling by the twilight shores of Niuyi. As a guest, I speak these words of parting, mindful of my own leisurely sentiments;
the past affairs of the Six Dynasties resonate through both present and antiquity, lingering especially upon the bells atop the Changgan Pagoda.

Master Fushang of Donglin carries a fathom-long cold tree across his shoulders with an iron staff; his eyes are chilled by the miasmic rains of the southern wilderness. Before even entering the gate, he has already discerned the truth:
the fragrance of his patched robe is stained with the lotuses of Jinchi.

A single kind of numinous root from Tangxi differs from the spring breeze; winding and winding, cold waters flow, their reflections emptying the sky. Who would believe that the fragrance upon the branches is so scarce?
Even the Elder of Huanhua has failed to appraise it.

The numinous earth of the mossy courtyard offers auspicious signs as purple blossoms soften; upon the jade steps they stand tall, their brilliance unrestrained. Their exquisite beauty is fit for consumption, their fame worthy of pride;
even a foot of land on Mount Shang is richer than a tower of jade.
In the Western Region of Zhuhang, who is worthy to inherit the orthodox lineage? This One Dharma is difficult to present to you. In broad daylight, I come in vain; those who understand me are few.
My shoulders are chilled by the heavy clouds of the Five Indies.
The jade axe has fashioned the moon-house through countless autumns; cold radiance floats within the palace of Guanghan.
Its gates and portals are vast and unobstructed, providing a canopy for all humanity.

The snow-covered village stretches far and wide, the great earth devoid of center or periphery; frost locks the thatched eaves, ten thousand *li* away from the heavens. I recall the seven taverns of the Dragon Inn;
in the night’s cold, my traveler’s pillow could not bring sleep.
To show those who revere the Way of Wisdom:
wisdom cannot know it, and knowledge is likewise difficult. A mere hair’s breadth of involvement blocks the heavy gates;
mountain flowers like brocade balls line the path—know for whom they are smiling as one face is broken open.
The monk Ba of Yuezhou transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* with his own blood and requested a verse;

I have interpreted its meaning according to the scripture. Like a snail crawling along a wall, the seven similes and three cycles form a cluster of blood where flies gather. Blowing away the withered flowers, fresh and beautiful ones rain down;
the scattered red petals fall upon the paper-stalks of the Shan River.
Master He, in the fifth month, went west along the river;
the river flows westward as snowy waves fly. The cold resentment in his breast he knows only within himself.
Having swallowed both the pit and the skin, he will surely return beneath the *litchi* tree.
When the snow clears atop Qinwang Peak, Master Qin returns;
The opportune moment before one’s eyes is difficult to change through antiquity or today. Below the Shrine of Right Military General, the mountains are washed clean;
A flying brush without a point cools the inkstone pool.

The snowy heart and withered wood are flecked with spring’s jade blossoms; heaven and earth are frozen solid, how long shall they remain congealed? Who need concern themselves with the cold hues of the Patriarchal Hall?
Every inch of liver and entrails is an inch of water.
The eminent Master returns to his hometown;
we rely on one another in this cool, secluded summer retreat. The flower-root lacks splendor, and the tiger has no stripes.
As he departs, he deliberately stirs up the matter; the master’s staff is not idle this very day.
Master Te went to Jiangxi to pay homage at Huangluo Mountain;
the mountain trees were shrouded in twilight. His cooking cloth was not yet stained by idle clouds. The Dharma cave of West River is famous throughout the world;
it is neither a herd of oxen nor a herd of horses.
The Venerable Vinaya Master traveled to Tiantong in Zhejiang;
in the spring warmth, jade resounds from the bottom of the ravine. Looking east toward the layered cliffs, the sun slants over the sea. The path enters amidst heaped clouds and cold, verdant hues;
look at the fruit of the emerald peach, do not look for its flowers.

The iron of Jian-tan is cold and lusterless, yet it harbors much ancient spirit; its shadow chills as it reflects alone upon the clear waves. Its thousand-fathom, sky-reaching breath is difficult to suppress;
like a single trace of autumn water, the frost cannot wear it away.
Tian Weina returns to Donglin to visit his master;
the lion has no teeth, yet his father possesses heavy tusks. The dragon-steed reflects its image upon the muddy banks. The spirit of the Jin dynasty has not ceased for a thousand ages;
fragrant white lotuses bloom across a pool of flowers.
The wall-dwelling Chan practitioner returns to the ancestral path in Qiantang;
how can one speak of such desolation? I cannot bear the regret that it vanishes like a trailing cloud. Who understands the intent of biting the arrowhead before the wind?
This arrow was shot by the King of Qian across the tide.
The Elder of Mount Shan at the Upper End has received the Dharma robes of Master Yue-lin;

he seeks a verse for his meditation cell on Mount Dan, which is situated wherever he may be. Regarding this matter, people say it is quite long: "Who would entrust a branch of the moon from the forest?
The *kāṣāya* still carries the fragrance of the osmanthus."
Master Tufu returns to Taiping;
after the rain has passed, the mountain mists part. The layered tortoises, upon seeing him, shake their heads and turn away. The sound of the horn once disturbed the dreams of Zen monks;
whose house is near the tower? Do not listen for the plum blossoms.
The Head Seat of Lantian wanders through Jiantian;
the jade fields of Lantian reflect the vermilion mountains. The sword-spirit is difficult to subdue, its piercing chill shooting toward the Dipper. Through ages, the streams and mountains remain;
through ages, the regrets persist. At twilight, do not lean upon the bridge’s railing.
In mourning for the Venerable Yuejian of Jianfu, his name remains inscribed upon the monument;
who shall gather these vast and empty phrases from the sky of Chu? The shadow of the long fishing pole grows cold upon the snowy traces of the rapids;
the mountain stream is silent, and the moon shines on its own.
Master Kang travels through the main thoroughfares of Western Zhejiang, drifting freely as he pleases.
Autumn enters the empty forest and the leaves are half-fallen. A single speck of Wu clouds adds to the traveler’s sorrow;
the temple bells, long and short, accompany the tides of the river.
Lamenting Master Yuetting of Mount Jiang:

Where he attained realization, how could he have ever betrayed the Buddha-mind? Now that he has retired to till his fields, the resentment remains difficult to settle. From now on, the path to Zhongshan Temple will fall into ruin;
the autumn colors are desolate, with but a single courtyard of moonlight.
The recorded notes on travels through Zhejiang, copied from paper wrappers, lack spiritual efficacy; on the road, sealed grievances and bitter sorrows weigh upon the heart.
Though the ginger from the Snowy Mountains is tasteless, it burns one’s intestines with the deepest venom.

Scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants strain their arms at the examination halls, where they first see their names upon the posted list; many who soar to high office once rose from the plow and hoe. Now, among those who hold official emoluments, there are many with extraordinary skills:
the selling of flower seedlings is prized, while the selling of books is held cheap.
For long the constellation Kui has obscured its cold radiance with both civil and martial arts, medicine, and divination. Having failed in my studies of the sword, my hair is already white.
With the four seas scarred by wounds and no medicine to heal them, I mostly rely on the shell of the tortoise to decide the rise and fall of dynasties.

Fisherman, woodcutter, plowman, and herdsman—having cast their silk lines, they float upon the waters. Idly parting the lingering clouds, they gather fallen pines. The clamor of the *jirang* song fills the ears of the aged;
the warmth of the peach grove rolls with the wind through the paulownia trees.
The lute, chess, calligraphy, and painting;
the strings resonate with the *Nanxun* wind as all things flourish. A new board reveals the wise and the foolish; mountains and rivers across the world form a single chronicle.
Seeking swift steeds of extraordinary power, many are pressed at the gate.

Little master Rulin, as you travel abroad at dawn, offer incense and take your leave before the Snow Mountain. Just then, the autumn rains have cleared and the sky is bright; go thus to Hubei and Hunan.
For one traveling abroad, the first thing is not to engage in Zen meditation.

Tilling the soil in seclusion amidst vast, brambly thorns that pierce the eyes; one fears that the concealment of one’s surname and escape from fame will not yet cease. The deeds of one’s ancestors regarding fields and gardens lie dormant in their contracts;
with a single plow, wind and rain bring back the autumn of heaven.
Jing-stones fall in profusion;
it is difficult to distinguish the true from the false. By whom can the mysterious essence be analyzed to reveal its fundamental nature? Buan He has grown old, his azure eyes dimmed;
white clouds add their shadows, embracing the traces of spring.
Kuai pays his respects at Shangren’s Jingshan, while concurrently addressing Master Xugou:
In the midst of a drenching storm, we struggled to reach you in haste. In this entire age, you are the sole Dragon Gate. The moment he saw the meditation seat, he overturned it.
This sword is but the scar left behind after Huang Chao passed through.
The Way of Eternal Quiescence seeks verse;
it is silent yet eternally illuminating, and that illumination returns to non-being. To investigate this, one must clarify the upward-moving faculty.
Since the moment of the Buddha’s smile at Vulture Peak, the tender crimson has not ascended the branches of fallen blossoms.
Inscribed on a Half-Sized Black Silk Undergarment for Daoist Attire by Lü Dongbin: Within the casket, the cosmic qi contains a cold radiance. The sun and moon of Penglai are idly difficult to guard;
the trees grow old south of the city, yet the wine remains fragrant.
Master Ming returns to Zifu in Gutian (the Dharma-seat of Attendant Shan).
After seeing him off, Ciming returned to his hometown and instructed his attendant to convey these words: "Beside this seat, the mountain has no fine flavor;
take out the hū-bread from the oven and blow upon the fragrant rice."
Diao Tai opens for Master Shangren;
with a single-shoulder patchwork robe, he descends from Longtai. With surplus funds, he buys straw sandals. To those who ask for news from Nanmin, he says:
"The *pianjianzhi* flower blooms amidst the snow."
Master Yi returns to Jiankang;
by the tea at Bāngshàn, our parting words are filled with deep affection. As a guest in foreign soil, it is ultimately difficult to divide between two lands.
At the residence of the Song Prime Minister atop Ye, the temple bell occasionally stirs the clouds of Bāngshàn.
The Master Wen’s title is "Brook of Brocade";
its current winds along the banks, soaking the bright rosy clouds. Who in this world can distinguish where the hemp is being soaked? With a single stroke of the loom, all phenomena are gathered in;
do not say that cutting water cannot produce flowers.
From the Great Chan Master on the Huai River, looking west toward Tiantai, the Huai marshes lie across a vast and misty void.
A solitary figure at the edge of the world accompanies but a single staff. Tomorrow, with his fly-whisk in hand, he will proceed along the road past the Pavilion;
gazing upon the waterfall piercing the clouds, he remains as but a lone monk.
When the Master Chuan traveled abroad to bid farewell, his parting words were drawn out like a long conversation. Possessing the eye of a pilgrim, it was as clear as frost;
in the land of Min, few wildcats travel the road—only the soaring hawks are the masters of the clan.
Serving the Hall and purifying the hair, you await your imperial summons;

seeking the finest artistry, your family tradition outshadows those of your peers. Long ago your blade flew forth, its cold edge containing a hidden radiance. O mountain monk, not even a single hair or pore can deceive you;
though there are no śarīra relics here, there is indeed frost.

Presented to the monk who crafts sandals, awaiting imperial summons in the style of the Shifun era, with the lake and mountains as his domain: The seams and lines must never be omitted or made too loose. In a single stride, the man of high attainment possesses a wondrous art:
With hands behind his back, he treads upon the clouds like a soaring phoenix.

The ox is tethered within an iron enclosure.
Li Bai:
The winds and dust of the six realms have not yet been swept clear; his sea-like wine-stomach breaks down the city of sorrow.
As the moon sinks at Chaisai and the tide-mark falls, it seems as though his poetic soul remains drunk and unawakened.

Du Fu, grieving for his country and its people, dwells as a guest in a distant province. Amidst the sound of frontier flutes, the autumn descends upon the watchtowers. At the Huantua Village, the cold floods have made the stream’s current thick;
it cannot wash away even a handful of sorrow from the winds and dust.
Dongpo:
What reliance can there truly be on gain and loss in this world? They are like floating flowers in the void or water in the sunlight. The Sea of Jade knows not that its body is but a guest;
throughout life, I have been accustomed to being a monk of the waters and clouds.

In the mountain valleys by the Fu River, the late autumn sun sinks low and vast. This exile wanders in leisurely verse, his sentiments long and deep. Before and after this life is but a single meal’s dream;
the fish sauce grows cold while the cassia wafts its fragrance.

Title: Grapes The slanting glow plays upon the golden tenderness; Scissors-cutting cold, the autumn vineyard. Thirsty souls would grow drunk on the juice; In dreams, one wanders through Xiliang Prefecture.
Emerald leaves are damp with dew-pearls’ fragrance; Shadows cast by the jade-white moon. The crystal curtains are chill; Who can summon the immortal guests?

Painted crabs descend upon the sand as the tide falls at the marsh; they scuttle and lumber about with clumsy grace. Whose wine-soaked fancy stirs such dreams? The wind through the reeds and leaves clash in the cold.
They strain their eyes for their sideways gait; turned askance, they reveal the sky beneath the waves. While the world boils like a cauldron of fire, none reach the edge of these withered lotuses.

The painted hawk with its iron-like beak snarls in rage, while golden threads dangle from its soft plumage. Its heroic spirit and noble bearing seem to long for flight; with a single upward glance of frosty eyes, it would slay foxes and hares.
Upon the level marshes, blood cools as the autumn descends upon the passes and rivers.

In the Lotus Society painting, the landscape is shrouded in wild smoke, an ancient border of Jin. Those who have joined the society return to it as the years and months are forgotten. Profits and honors cannot entangle their dreams of the incense burner;
amidst the shadows of lotus flowers, the sound of the water clock drags on long.
The Painting of Peach Blossom Spring:
The painted streams and mountains suffice for all four neighbors; bright clouds obscure the cave entrance in spring.
Had it not been for the fisherman’s oar blowing away the stinking nets, the peach blossoms would have grown old alone, weary of Qin.
Staying at Xiangcheng, I recall ascending with Elder Sheng by the ancient stream;

deep into the night and in stillness, we deliberated together. That which permeates the heavens and scorches the earth is but a tiny fragment—flowers bloom in dense profusion within the layered city, carrying the fragrance of snow.
The junior monk bowed to Attendant Zhou and requested a verse for his *Discernment of the Recorded Sayings*.
My words are worn and stale, lacking the spark of life; I have burdened you with this for several months of compilation and publication.
Only when the windows are plastered and the curtains drawn shall these recorded sayings finally begin to circulate.

The severed arrowhead makes its path difficult to trace; in a flash, one must pivot upon the single mechanism of birth and death. You must realize this directly and with urgency.
Should you hesitate even for a moment—(he throws down the fire)—it is like wrapping wet paper around a flame.

flawless and peerless, it has been buried for ninety-five years. To the very end, with a single blow, it is all together.

they were bound by the gravity of their dharma-kinship and the intimacy of their personal affection. Through scolding and harsh rebukes, he refined you to completion. Though Peng Xiu’s life was short and his years ended prematurely, his legacy remains.
With a fixed number of hand-movements, cast off the entanglements of attachment; harbor no fear or dread. Herein lies the severing of the bond between teacher and disciple;
herein also lies the forgetting of the affection between flesh and bone. (Casting fire) Within the flames, the wooden man sheds tears like rain.
Regarding the cremation of Dharma-relative Fu, the Head Seat:
his words were sincere and trustworthy, and his conduct was firm and upright. To perceive him through his external manifestations is easy; to know him within his inner emptiness is difficult.
That he passed away while seated, as smoke rose from the incense burner, is not without precedent. But how do you understand the intention of our late teacher?
"Silence! It would be better to swallow charcoal than to let the fire of the Imperial Treasury [of the Dharma] escape.

Little Master Tan, the attendant, served the Fire for three years with jade-like flawlessness.
Eighteen springs end as one lingering dream. The dream is broken, the dust is cleared—what remains of grace and duty?
Severance. The *udumbara* flower blooms uniquely within the fire.
Regarding the fire at the Dharma Vice-Abbot’s quarters, Preceptor Neng did not abandon a single dharma within the sphere of Buddhist practice;
though he calculated and deliberated a thousand times over ten thousand ways, it was obtained through sheer persistence and born of sheer effort.
What limit is there? Prajñā has no boat; Bodhi has no shore. Today, first practice the contemplation of fire.

the pure person’s fire is bright and clear.

The Ritual Master Yan enters the stupa to advance on the Way and adorn his person;
he casts aside names to pursue reality. When the lamp-bowl at the stone window drifted down, what were those illusions, bubbles, and empty flowers?

Jiwei, when leaves fall they return to the root—this reveals what is intimate. A flower blooms within the fire, its color like iron.

At the moment of overturning the monastery of *Pūrṇabhadra*, what then? (He throws fire. Let the flames spread with the wind.

In the meditation hall there is no fire, for the mind has severed all攀緣 (pān-yuan, clinging to objects). In the Way there is neither cultivation nor realization; yet to mistake appearances for reality is to lose one's head, leaving the entire body in sickness.
[For] such-and-such a person, the *campaka* flower blooms and the iron tree is fragrant in spring; its brilliance does not follow the wind, and when the fire is extinguished, it remains.
The "Monstrous Stone" Chief Seat Holder:

A piece of firewood and a wooden board hang across the eaves—world-transcending, lofty, and ancient. When one lets go of empty space and walks forth, the mountains and rivers of the great earth have not a square inch of soil remaining.
One thing is eternally enlightened, never falling into birth and death. (He throws down the fire. Amidst the shadows of the fiery clouds, the Monstrous Stone is revealed.

The Bureau Chief presides over fire and secretly maneuvers the pivot of the mechanism; yet he has not forgotten his limited capacity. He calculates with a thousand thoughts and ten thousand reckonings, arriving at his conclusions through deliberation.

Thus, the ignorance of birth and death only increases his deluded imaginings. As for that single phrase, "not falling into thought or mental conception"—how would you deal with it? (He throws the fire.)
Fire is said to blaze upward.
The Venerable Rui understood the subtle signs of fire;

such is its spiritual nature. Only through such wisdom does one become a sage. To call this "attaining the degree" is to leave the mind empty; it is not yet the realization attained through a fixed term.
When overturning the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment, what then? (He throws fire. Fire emerges and the wood is exhausted.
Elder Long, the fire spreads across the great earth until it is level;
the void becomes hollowed out. Treading upon the dead sea, the waves overturn the sky; the clay ox is startled up, its two horns meeting.
The horn is broken; it is distinct from the distinct. (He throws down the fire. Hiding water within the sun; fishing for turtles amidst the flames.

With a good supervisor and grain-fire, and a virtuous nature and benevolent heart, one clearly understands the cause and recognizes the fruit. When one reaches the moment of winnowing the chaff to find the rice, one awakens to the intoxication of the yellow millet dream.
The dream is shattered. When departing in this very manner, what then? (He throws fire. A tortoise facing the fire.

Because he supervised the grain and counted the rice and measured the firewood, he sought to compensate for his faults through diligence and exhausted all thieving thoughts. One must urgently attain sudden enlightenment. Why? Because of the wind.
Blowing out the fire:
when the junior monk first approached the Senior Elder’s fire, it was vast and profound.
The ultimate principle is deep and abyssal; if one realizes it, it encompasses everything before one's eyes; if one does not realize it, one drifts through birth and death.
Silent. The relationship between teacher and disciple has been severed; the profound path is difficult to trace. For now, let us distinguish true gold from within the fire.
Elder Xiweng, what is this Brahma-sound coming from the West Hall?
What image does ultimate emptiness possess? Disperse the assembly and travel to various quarters; only through this will you ultimately attain clarity regarding birth-and-death and ignorance.
The false and delusory increases all the more. Why? Because fire does not flourish in the west.
When Chan Master Zhang (who formerly resided at the monastery named Jinxī) was my Head Seat, he had already attained liberation;
the waves of the Jinxu stream have long since flowed away, for my Head Seat has already set out on his travels. Guì.

The jade scepter must also be re-polished; the Way transcends merit and achievement, while sentiment is forgotten in the mirror-like awakening. (Throws fire) The flames grow cold in the red furnace as snowflakes fall.
[End of] Head Seat Huo (formerly resided at Cui-lin and Qing-xi).

To speak of human affairs: the green forest casts its reflection upon the encircling clear stream; the mechanism of the precipitous cliff is pressed into action. Cold springs surge, clamoring through the ancient ravine;
the mundane realm is empty and still, utterly devoid of permanence. Earth, water, fire, and wind are truly but illusions.
But as for Muzhou receiving Yunmen and succeeding Xuefeng—how is that? (He throws a torch. Sending charcoal in the midst of snow.
In the past, Master Huairang of Huangmei transmitted the Dharma but did not transmit the robe; today, Xuefeng transmits the robe but does not transmit the Dharma.

Whether this is the Dharma or not the Dharma, there is no difference to be seen. As for the dead word and the living word, they are known only by oneself. (He throws down the fire. What need is there to hold a torch?
An Inscription for a Lover.
Together with the Fire-Official (who died in the bath), their voices resonate in harmony.
Flying the sacred arrow, the full edge is secretly revealed. Only those on the same path shall know. Late evening, the dark assembly.
Concealing poison within, though in the land of non-arising, one turns over with a single laugh; yet in the sea of birth and death, one has not yet escaped defilement and turbidity.
(Thrusting forth fire) How can bathing in water compare to bathing in fire?
The weeds before the Hall of Shaving the Hair are the weeds of ignorance. When they are completely cleared away, all colors return to black. In the coral grove, the moon shines brightly;
when the blade is raised, its cold light blazes forth. Having been utterly cleansed and removed, not even a hair’s breadth remains. A single [blade] amidst the snow.
The flower blooms in five petals.

Entrusting the robe (along with six others attached), at the foot of Cock’s Foot Mountain and at Huangmei, they meet in secret and cast themselves into the light; there is neither right nor wrong. When the whole body bears the heavy responsibility, it is as if—
What? Six people have become great vessels;
a single thread binds a heavy burden. It is transmitted without being transmitted; one must seek the hidden meaning. The secret lies with you. Handing over the *kāṣāya*, he said:
"The *kāṣāya* is draped over the shoulder."
Self-Praise for Elder Guangfawen of Chaozhou, Requesting Praise: The Dharma cannot be transmitted;
these words were written without further revision. Transmitted by Yongyuan, who is as clumsy in learning as I am in folly. Based on the Way of the Snow Mountains.
His benevolence was universal, and his fame shook the lands beyond the sea. A recent report states that in the depths of the lake, the eyes of the crocodiles flash like lightning.

Elder Ding of Sanfeng requested a eulogy for one who sat enthroned in golden robes and discoursed on emptiness with a jade whisk; he established the school’s doctrine just as Yunmen had with Wenyuan. He propagated its...
The Way is like Huanglong’s relation to Ciming: dwelling in the mountains with the ancient rigor of former masters, yet lacking the worldly adaptability of the present age;
holding the scales and weights beyond the realm of measurement, while lacking the cord and ruler within his breast.
With such peerless character, who could possibly follow in his footsteps? Three peaks rise above the clouds toward the azure firmament.
Elder Yunmen Bin requests a eulogy:

His Way transcends past and present; his spiritual faculty is fully capable of both killing and giving life. He laughed when Master Zeng ladled out the assembly of fifteen hundred; the wooden ladle was simply too short.
Baiyang sent away thirteen men; the bamboo rakes were too short. Neither color nor sound—filling the ears and filling the eyes.
A single song from Yunmen: the river breeze is warm.
Venerable Shiming, when requested to praise the capacity for awakening, you remained silent;
in your application, you were profound and obscure. You were accustomed to using a broken tendon to stir the Luo River; you nailed the void without so much as a single inch of wood.
It is both real and false; it is neither form nor sound. A bright moon fills half the window, with the shadows of plum blossoms cast across it.

At the request of the Elder Guizhang of Xiaoying Temple, he was praised as being stern and difficult to approach, yet warm, kind, and easy to behold. He traveled through Zhejiang to seek the Way and search for teachers, then returned to Min, where he received [transmission].
At Xuanzhai Monastery, he expanded the Way of the Great Center; penetrating the profound and subtle mysteries, he continued the lamp of Xueqiao, its radiance manifesting clearly.
Who could exhaust the excellence of his teacherless wisdom? Having a son who truly upholds the family tradition, it was fitting that he should find worthy successors.
A single drop of cold spring water waves against the heavens.
At the request of the Elder Xingfu Yu, this eulogy is offered:

His spirit and bearing are leisurely and serene; his countenance is rugged and formidable. A white-marked tiger emerging from the forest—its stench of blood cannot be concealed. With gnashing teeth and a tortoise-like snout, he stands majestic.
The miasma of poison is at its peak; it cannot be fully described. Blue surpasses the indigo; its brilliant starlight outshines the southern heavens.
Chan Master Chuzang requested a eulogy for his portrait.

My wisdom is not received through a teacher’s instruction, yet my learning is focused and earnest. I release the "Turtle-Nose" from the Southern Mountains and capture the "Crocodile" alive from the Southern Sea.
Appearing in such a manner, who could possibly accompany him? How could one bear to see these bare hands holding the Celestial Scripture?
Disciple Zhengxin, Abbot Zangzhu, requests a eulogy for one whose mouth is venomous yet whose heart is compassionate;
whose breath is stern and whose countenance is ancient. He is a successor to Yongyuan who does not recognize the Buddha-mind, yet he has received the imperial decree to proclaim it forth.
Your Majesty, you possess the proportions of a whole mansion within your breast, yet lack a name that startles the world.
What need is there to portray yourself before others? It would be like seizing a sheep to prove its father.
My nephew, the head monk Zhengshao, requested a eulogy for Yuan, who was distant yet cool when approached, yet warm when drawn near;
he continued the lineage of the Guangling Way, his dispersed tones harmonizing with the Shao melody, and he protected the teachings until their extinction at Mount Zhongfeng.
The sand-basin is shattered; the orthodox lineage of Weiyang has its source. A single drop of cold spring water divides into the four seas.
Mei Shi, Song Xuanjiao’s true eulogy:
"The Goose Pagoda is without intent; the rooster-window has purpose. A hundred years remain an illusion, yet one stands proud amidst the dregs of the age—the essence of the Three Teachings."

Profound indeed! He has thoroughly illuminated the single principle; his liver and entrails are as hard as iron and stone, difficult to shift even unto old age. Throughout his life, only the plum blossoms have known his heart’s intent.
—Eulogy for Master Jinma of Pingcun Village, by Li Jun.

With a rhinoceros-horn cap atop his head and eyebrows as elegant as *zhī* fungi, he sought seclusion within the layered walls of the capital. Trading books for a dwelling, he composed the "Return to Pan Valley.

He channeled springs and excavated ponds; his dream-like existence suddenly awakened, yet the world of men was no longer what it had been. The peach blossoms of the Hidden Village shroud the spring branches, branch after branch.
Eulogy for the Honorable Professor Chen Hengxiu by Shan Yun.

Sparse and elegant like clouds over the mountains; clear and bright as the moon reflected in a pool. Poetry and ritual are passed down through his lineage, such that the ritual seats are warm with springtime grace.

He welcomes scholars from across the lakes and seas, so that the Chen mansion is bright with the light of day. A model for later students, he remains a mature and accomplished elder of this ancient house. Huguang.
Towering trees reach for the clouds in their azure height.
This is the portrait of Master Fangyan of Dongchan, whose rocky visage inspires awe.
Lofty and eminent, he was distinguished and outstanding; his laughter and discourse dissolved the boundaries beyond the mundane world, his brilliance transcending all of today.

The strategic maneuvers of that time: dwelling idly amidst mountain clouds, their shadows naturally unfurling and retracting; the moon over the city of Awakening shines its radiance across seas and mountains.
Beneath every phrase lies the artistry of painting; before every movement, there is the act of sketching. Layer upon layer, mist and water darken the towers and pavilions.
Seeing off the Head of the Dry-Store (Gan Weina) as he travels abroad:

Heaven and earth span the present and the past; sun and moon shine bright. Mountains and rivers do not change with the passing of postal relays. Shoulders rub and heels touch in a world reeking of dust and smoke.

The sands are empty, the Han River cold, and the phoenixes vanish into the dark. Before the peach blossoms in the grotto reach spring, the leaves have already fallen. How many times has the wild grass witnessed the frost?
Amidst the dense green, the wall-base resounds with the rhythmic thumping of the staff; the back of the straw sandals is crisscrossed with the *yuanyang* lacing.
There is not a single word to be taken along. The clear clouds cast their reflections, overturning the dark depths of the pool.
Seeing the Monk Jian off on his return to Yanzhou:
A single staff leaves the winding stream at dawn; In the cool sky, a rain has gathered the lingering dampness. "How is the Dharma-way of Xuefeng these days? "He simply says:
'When the porridge is sufficient, the rice is also sufficient. The patch-robed monk has no striving and no desire; His own water-buffalo [is free]..."
Tending the flock at home; both seeking fame and seeking emolument are vast and obscure. The moon bathes the banks of the Yan River as he half-catches jade.
Master Ning returns from Quanzhou; Snowy Turtle Head is but a handful from heaven.
Coming from the south, coming from the north, it is difficult to find a mooring. The old tortoise-nose of the South Mountain grinds on.
The tusk: A white-browed tiger with horns on Mount Nan; as soon as the Master saw him, he turned his face toward him. How could the licorice ever have been lightly moved?
When the black staff was snapped in two, he reached home; the moon was cold in Luoyang as the tide-mark fell.
Master Shou returns to Hangzhou;
having long been parted from the West Lake, he comes with a single staff for a journey to the Southland. Everywhere the green mountains are filled with the clamor of nesting thorns;

at every turn, the towers and pavilions see the crows settling in the dusk. The cold spring has stilled its voice as iron dragons slumber; the old moss upon the withered trees thickens in the late spring.
The flowers are gathered. You must investigate for yourself; hasten to apply yourself. Who shall uphold the Great Dharma as the orthodox lineage?
When the flower of the mind suddenly blossoms, the fragrance of the cassia seeds fills the gourd-bowl and the moon is as bright as day.
Master Mingzang returned to Chaoyang to visit his teacher;

he had previously parted from me at the summit of Mount Ao. Now, seeing you again after more than ten years, I see your solitary staff chilled by the rains of Beishan, and your woolen robes fragrant with the lotuses of West Lake.
Worn out by wandering, you have lost the desire for excursions through Wu and Chu; your dreams of home fly back toward the south.
At the edge of the clouds: those who travel to seek the Dharma should value the manifestation of the ultimate matter. There is no need to present the circular symbol before the Master;

old Yu’s pure兴致 (xìng) cannot be reached, yet the miasmic fog does not obstruct his suspended pair of eyes. The lamp-light in Han Gong’s study is still; the dark green of the Tang-era cypress must surely reach toward heaven.
The former Abbot Xian was sent to rebuild the Nārāyaṇa Cave;
the Dharma-cave of the South stands as the first transmission of the nameless (Avijñapti) Dharma Master. Ciyun’s aspirations were not fulfilled, and wild clouds disperse;

the *Avataṃsaka* flowers deeply dye the mountain blossoms fresh. The wooden *tāla* drum frequently locks the ancient sounds of Indian scriptures, while the whale-shaped pestle occasionally shakes the azure heavens.
Longmian: In the secluded mountain chambers, the morning light is dim; the simple practitioner clutches warmth against the cold while practicing solitary meditation.

With a bronze pitcher, he draws the emerald water of the pool under the moon; with a clay steamer, he strikes sparks to burn pine smoke for incense. Reaching thousands of villages and myriad hamlets by following his feet, he need not discuss the three coins at the tip of his staff.
Within these crags, the scenery is sublime and transcends the divine; when shall I take my staff and ascend to the highest peak? — Jingtai (Scripture Terrace)
Grant me a moment’s leisure for a smile; my old passion reaches out its hand to stroke the blue heavens.
A humble attendant seeks to travel afar, yet foolish clouds obscure the sky in bitter gloom.
The flowers of the Garden of Awakening have withered, the cold hues are harsh, and the misty waters of a hundred cities are but empty traces.
Vast and empty. Wherever Good Wealth (Sudhana) looks, he loses the pavilion. This morning a guest arrived from Chaoyang; in the waves of the crocodile sea, its head and horns are visible.
Whose jar of pickled vegetables must be the deepest? He seeks me everywhere for a single phrase of instruction. I wish to write it down, yet there is no word to be sketched or modeled.
Cold and desolate beneath the four eaves, the flowers fall from the rafters.

Arriving at Fangshan Temple, the peaks stand firm on every side like a screen. Wild colors float with a glossy luster; springs and rocks are pure and clear. The seeds of the *shetong* tree shed their husks as the morning dew grows cold;

the pods of the wild bean burst open, releasing their autumn fragrance. Snakes in the village and rats in the droppings lie beneath one’s feet; this place is utterly secluded from the mundane world, shrouded in mist.
Dust and stench have vanished; my arrival seems to have accorded with a subtle appointment. My voice calls and the myriad phenomena respond as the celestial wind whistles.
Worthy sights and scenes brighten both eyes; through half the window, the mountain clouds are green and the sunlight shines.
Yangshan Yan recorded this for the Abbot of Jingshan: "In years past, he once drank from the cup of ginger and apricot.
Fragrance drifted through the snowy valley like rolling light thunder. At the south city wall, the auspicious bell revealed his brilliance and refinement;

not a single blade of grass dared vie for the vanguard of spring. When the tide subsides, the three mountains dwell in the twilight mist; when the rain closes in, the pavilions and towers are shrouded in gloom."
The stench of dust settles as I set out on my journey; the sound of the axe has just ceased. With intention in mind, when shall the bright window be opened?
Filled with the old grievances of Wu and Chu, autumnal thoughts enter my dreams without delay. At Longmen, a generation strives to emulate those who look up in reverence;
to recruit the worthy, they are now building the Golden Terrace.
The Venerable Baoshou of Zhongyuan visited Jingci;

his every step was a smile as he traversed the clouds of Wu and Chu. That he made two mistakes during this summer need not be discussed; within his sleeves he possessed the true value of Central China.
His refined and pure nature—who could dissect its rootless mystery? The green mountains never end the traveler's path; the pavilions and towers stand deep-shut—whom would they welcome?
The family lineage: Cold golden waves surge, the traces of water-mallow merge; plum fragrance and willow shadows fill the empty dusk.
Chan Master Nan returns to Zhejiang;
mountain streams resound with autumn sounds distinct and clear. Black rocks rub the clouds, their color like iron; withered trees hold spring, the night fixed in stillness.
Return! The square pond dabs the moon, containing a void of azure; the vast ocean-treasury opens wide, with flowers layered upon layers.

The true mechanism is performed and then retracted; he who holds its key has found a worthy person. Not only does he possess power, he must also possess substance. The *kang*, *nan*, *qi*, and *zi* trees serve as the pillars and beams of the Dharma;

the fire-dates and persimmons are intended to replace the thorns. When his work is accomplished, he unfastens his seal amidst the autumn of the lake and mountains; the shadows of willows and plum trees [reflect the scene].
Fragrance is an old acquaintance; I, aged, dwell by the fiery clouds and the mountain streams and snows. Gazing toward Wu and Chu, my inspiration knows no limit;
facing the wind, I again seek a verse for your departure. A single word I wish to write, yet my brush hovers; from the jade ink-well, waves of water surge like a torrent.
The pines by the eaves waft their fragrance, their green needles seem as if they might drip.
The old Chan master of Penglai Chingshui Yuanan comes from within Chingshui Hermitage; his spirit carries the clarity of the spring water, free from a single speck of dust.

Since he first recognized the Master of the Hermitage, not a petal of a flower has stained the moss before the hut. Within his breast, there is a wondrous and responsive living dharma; he does not store even a grain of rice.

The straw mat and firewood; having grown old, he has settled his debt of pilgrimage. How many layers of cloth socks accompany the green shoes? At the gate of the ball court, there is no iron bolt or lock;
from the auspicious towers, auspicious mists and fragrant smoke unfold. The rising waves and plum rains stir the springs and ravines; leaning against the heavens, golden and azure towers soar aloft.
Though these fine mountains offer much to detain one, my returning boat must painfully follow the An River back home. The blazing clouds...
A single laugh at the outset brings life; where in the human world is there not Penglai?
Sent to Master Dongzhai of Chaozhou, a teacher of both ancient and modern religious traditions, Changli.
At the outset, you made your name renowned for literature along the coastal seas; the rites and music of the ancient ocean flourished under your transformative influence.

The earth: the miasmic rains have not washed away the stele of Mount Mei. The numinous power of the land offers auspicious omens, which Heaven does not withhold; brilliantly they illuminate the sea as the constellation Kui descends.

The name of the hall is "Eastern Admiration," for he admires Eastern Lu (the Spring and Autumn Annals); his heart for antiquity and his pursuit of the ancients cannot be shifted. In the assembly hall, he serves at the peak of the Tortoise (the imperial court), fulfilling his filial duty to the family;
with utmost eloquence, he speaks of public justice and discusses the poetry of the Duke. I, an old man deep in the woods, have hair like snow; when shall we ever meet?
Beholding him, his two brows are raised; clouds hang across the Iron Wall of Black Rock, and the ancient stream swells in rage, its spring waters lush.
Leaning against the wind, he brandishes his brush in vain longing; my heart, in a single measure, flies afar after the soaring summer clouds.

The Abbot of Wuzang traveled through Zhejiang; at that time, he mistakenly listened to a poem of minor elegance. Though the ocean of his treasury was overturned, it was difficult to wash the ears clean. When the dust of sound has vanished, the path of meaning is forgotten;
ancient and present merge into a single, profound principle. Amidst the clouds of Wu and the waters of Chu, pure inspiration flourishes; let one rest the eyes upon the rivers and mountains. Rest.

A Didactic Allegory: On level fields and shallow grass, one must remain vigilant; The great tiger has not yet reached old age where its teeth have fallen out. The river is empty and the year draws to a close—what time is this?
One’s power and resolve must be courageous and decisive, without delay. A single word spoken in the wind is difficult to commit to paper.
Snow gathers at the four eaves as plum blossoms fly.
The junior disciple, serving as the *vinaya-dhara*, departs for Zhejiang at dawn;

he offers this parting song to the Spring from the Deep Ravine. Grinding my teeth against the wind, I have no other exhortation to give: Chongyun, you who possess the will, must strive together to take flight.
Do not chase after the spring colors upon the rooftops. Write gāthās upon the mountain-river paper by the bright window, and let the cold drift away on the bamboo by the eaves.

Six flavors soar in all directions as the five tastes of the season steam their fragrance; this old monk has but a single flavor that he cannot bring forth. The formal study is concluded and the task finished, so I return;
by the earthen stove I wait for you to roast turnips.

A Gift for a Painter of Landscapes There is a guest, a guest who comes to the city’s corner, With a secret scroll of vermilion and green ink tucked within his sleeves. His conception seizes the pivot of the primal source of creation;

His brushwork exhausts the finest details of a single hair, down to the last grain of ink. I am ashamed that my deep forest life has left snow upon my brow; My coarse robes are coldly dyed with mountain hues.
Clouds shimmer; the rain falls upon the bamboo eaves, and pine smoke drifts thin through the pavilion. There is no need to unroll even half a scroll of fine silk.

He is not me, and I am not he. The great void is shadowless, like a vessel of clear ice. Though the mountain forests and the imperial court differ in their destinies, the Great Hand remains to paint his likeness in the Lingyan Gallery.
The bamboo chamber opens as the Head Seat returns to rebuild the Great Zhongzhu;
Wang-han Fang donned his robes amidst flowers falling like rain. The heavenly wind shears the water, the spring light melts. The characters on the stele above are worthy of the former sages;

the perilous cliff-edges of his verses press against the full edge of the pivot. For several years on the mountain peak, we have idly followed one another; every time I spoke to the utmost, I saw only his loftiness.

Our friendship is profound. Tall and upright, the bamboo grove stands by the cottage; dense and fragrant, the pine mountain wafts its scent. As we part this morning, our feelings are deep and lingering.
The clear waters flow afar, their cold currents rushing on. Between elder and younger brothers there is no distinction; with a smile at the gate, we meet in joy.
For having been long estranged from me, you have shown me great courtesy; I dare not trouble you with even a single sheet of paper, like a bird crossing the sky. I look forward to...
This Way is vast within the Great Center. The dragon in the deep pool leaps for joy at the mountain stream.
*The Recorded Sayings of Master Qiaoyin*, Volume Lower (End).
